sens: Failure, falling short in the fulfillment of a duty or task
Wrongdoing against a person, misdeed
Moral fault, transgression against God
Break, separation due to sin or rebellion
Rejection or denial of faith and covenant
G3900.detail:
1. In its basic sense, it is a misstep, a failure in fulfilling an obligation: something that should have been done or not done and was missed (Romans 5:15-18, where Adam's fault brings death to all).
2. It is also any reprehensible act, an offense against a person: when you have "something against someone," it is because they have committed an offense (Mark 11:25).
3. Ethically and spiritually, it is a moral fault, a transgression of God's law (Ephesians 1:7 speaks of the forgiveness of our sins through the blood of Christ).
4. In the relationship between God and His people, the offense also denotes the fall, the break: when Israel turns away, it is an offense that causes separation (Romans 11:11-12).
5. More broadly, it is the refusal or denial of God's grace, the rejection of the covenant through rebellion (Ephesians 2:1, 5: we were dead in our offenses).
G3900.origine: The Greek word παράπτωμα comes from παραπίπτω (para-piptô), composed of "para" (beside, wrong) and "piptô" (to fall, to stumble): to fall beside, that is, to stray from the right path, to commit a misstep. Originally, the image is physical (to trip, to fall), then it becomes moral (to err, to sin). In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the Greek word παράπτωμα primarily translates מַעַל (maʿal, betrayal, offense) and פֶּשַׁע (pesha, transgression). This word differs from ἁμαρτία (hamartia, sin as falling short of the goal): an offense is often a concrete act against someone, while sin is broader.
G3900.emploi: The word appears 19 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul's epistles. It is frequent in Romans (8 times) and Ephesians (3 times), as well as in Matthew and Mark when speaking of forgiveness. In the Gospels, it refers to the offenses done to us that we must forgive (Matthew 6:14-15, Mark 11:25-26): it is a concrete act that hurts someone and must be released. In the Pauline epistles, it takes on a broader theological significance: Adam's offense (his transgression, his fall) brought death to all (Romans 5:15, 18), while the act of righteousness of Christ brings justification and life. The offense can also refer to the rejection of Israel or rebellion against God (Romans 11:11-12, Ephesians 2:1, 5).
G3900.portee: This word reminds every believer that our faults and transgressions are forgiven by the blood of Christ (Ephesians 1:7), and that we have passed from spiritual death to life (Ephesians 2:1, 5). It also calls us to forgive the offenses of others as God has forgiven us (Matthew 6:14-15). More profoundly, it shows how a single act of rebellion (Adam's offense) has infected all humanity, but how the obedience of one (Jesus Christ) brings justification to all (Romans 5:18), giving forgiveness and redemption a universal dimension.

sens: To be carried away or swept along by a current, like things that slide or drift
Figuratively, to lose grip on something, to let slip what one possessed
To unknowingly abandon a truth or reality that one believed was secure
G3901.detail:
1. The word paints the image of an object being carried away by a current: it passes by what should hold it back, drifting away without one noticing. This is the sense of the Greek verb, which implies a continuous movement to the side and forward.
2. Applied to spiritual matters, being carried away means letting slip the understanding or attachment to a truth heard. One does not forget it abruptly; one gradually detaches from it, like a ship that drifts. Hebrews 2:1 is its only biblical usage: the danger of being carried away from the teachings of Christ.
3. The nuance is one of negligence and passivity: nothing is consciously rejected, but one allows oneself to be carried elsewhere. This is why the apostle urges to hold more firmly to the things heard.
G3901.origine: The word combines the prefix "para" (beside, along) and "rhéō" (to flow, to run). The image is that of a flow passing by: not a violent shock, but a slow and imperceptible drift. The root evokes the movement of water, hence the sense of slipping, flowing out of reach. In Hebrew, the verb "yaval" (Isaiah 44:4) carries the same idea of flow or current.
G3901.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 2:1. The author warns his readers against the danger of letting the heard Word drift away from them imperceptibly. It is a pastoral warning: it is not an active rejection of the Gospel that is in view, but rather the gradual negligence, the inattention that slowly widens the distance between the believer's heart and the truth he has received. The apostle therefore exhorts to a more vigilant attachment.
G3901.portee: This word reminds the reader that faith is not static. The gradual abandonment of a received truth is a real and silent danger, more subtle than open rebellion. It invites every Christian to examine whether they are allowing their understanding of the Gospel to drift, and to cultivate a conscious and renewed attachment to what they have heard from Christ.

sens: figure or emblem painted on the bow of a ship to identify it
distinctive mark placed on an object
G3902.detail: 1. The ship's emblem is the visible figure or emblem painted on the side or bow of a boat to identify and recognize it at sea. In Acts 28:11, the ship that carries Paul bears the emblem of "the Dioscuri" (Castor and Pollux), two deities often represented on Greek ships as protectors of sailors. This distinctive mark allows one to distinguish a ship from others. 2. More broadly, the word denotes any mark or sign painted, engraved, or affixed to an object to signal or characterize it.
G3902.origine: The Greek word comes from the root "sēma" (σῆμα) which means mark, sign. The prefix "para" (παρά) indicates what is "beside," "next to," hence the original idea of "marked beside" or "marked on the side." The starting image is that of a visible mark affixed to the side of an object for identification. The word has evolved from the sense of counterfeit or falsified (in classical Greek) to the sense of marked with a distinctive sign (in later texts).
G3902.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 28:11, during Paul's journey to Rome after his shipwreck in Malta. It specifically designates the emblem of the Alexandrian ship on which Paul and his companions embark to continue their journey: the Dioscuri (Castor and Pollux). This precise detail shows that Luke, the author of Acts, was attentive to the particulars of the ships of his time and their distinctive marks, enhancing the credibility of his travel narrative.
G3902.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible places importance on the concrete details of the ancient world and the daily lives of believers. It does not spiritualize everything: it also cares about material realities like ships and their marks. For the Christian, this shows that Paul continued his ministry by traveling on ordinary trade routes, carrying the message of Christ in a familiar and real world.

sens: To arrange and organize something so that it is ready for use
To set up the necessary conditions or means before an action
To have the disposition or equipment to face a circumstance
G3903.detail:
1. The verb denotes the concrete action of preparing something, like a meal: one arranges, organizes what is necessary. In Acts 10:10, food is prepared for Peter, which means that the ingredients are arranged and cooked.
2. More broadly, "to prepare" means to create the conditions for a future action, to equip or arrange oneself before a circumstance arises. In 1 Corinthians 14:8, one who hears a confused trumpet sound cannot prepare for battle, meaning they cannot equip themselves and get ready to fight.
3. The word can also express the state of readiness or disposition: to be ready, to have in place what is appropriate. In 2 Corinthians 9:2-3, the Corinthians are prepared (ready) to give for the collection, meaning they have the willingness and likely the means mobilized.
G3903.origine: The Greek word combines the prefix "para" (beside, alongside) and a root meaning "to equip" or "to arrange." It evokes the idea of properly arranging things, placing them beside oneself or alongside oneself in view of a need. In Hebrew, the verb "érakh" (to arrange, to set in order) expresses a similar image. Words from the same Greek family revolve around this notion of arrangement and preparation.
G3903.emploi: The verb appears four times in the provided usages, always with the meaning of "to prepare" or "to be ready." In Acts 10:10, a meal is prepared: this is the immediate and concrete action. In 1 Corinthians 14:8, it is about preparing oneself, that is, getting ready to act. In 2 Corinthians 9:2-3, the word expresses the state of preparation, of voluntary availability in the face of an obligation (the collection for the saints in Jerusalem). In all cases, the context emphasizes that to prepare is to organize and mobilize what is necessary before the appointed time.
G3903.portee: This word invites the Christian to vigilance and diligence: faith is not a passive waiting, but an active disposition. Whether to serve in the assembly (1 Corinthians 14), to be generous (2 Corinthians 9), or simply to live day by day, the believer is called to "prepare," that is, to organize their strengths and means in accordance with God's will.

sens: Act of preparing, of putting in order
Equipment, what is prepared
Day of preparation before the Sabbath or a Jewish feast
G3904.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the action of preparing, of putting in order before an important event. It is a work of organization and prior arrangement.

2. It can also refer to the equipment itself, the things prepared and set in place for an activity or service.

3. In Jewish usage, this word takes on a very specific meaning: it designates the day preceding the Sabbath or a major feast, when the Jews prepared by completing all the work prohibited on the Sabbath day. All four Gospel writers use this term for the Friday of the crucifixion: Matthew 27:62 ("the day after preparation"), Mark 15:42 ("the eve of the Sabbath"), Luke 23:54 ("the day of preparation"), John 19:14 and 19:31 ("the preparation of the Passover"). This day is equivalent to Friday in the Jewish calendar.
G3904.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to prepare" with the prefix "para-" (beside, in view of). It expresses the idea of putting in order what is necessary. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it translates the Hebrew word עֲבֹדָה (avoda), which means "work, labor." The Gospels use it as a technical term to designate the fixed day of the Jewish week dedicated to preparations.
G3904.emploi: The word appears six times in the New Testament, exclusively in the four Gospels, all concentrated around the account of the passion of Jesus. Mark 15:42 explains clearly: the "preparation" is "the eve of the Sabbath." It is not simply the act of preparing, but an entire day in the Jewish calendar, the day when the Law prohibited creative work but when the Jews prepared for the Sabbath rest. John 19:14 further specifies "the preparation of the Passover," showing that this same day also encompassed the great feast of Passover. All four accounts use it to situate the crucifixion in time and explain the urgency of taking Jesus down from the cross before sunset (John 19:31).
G3904.portee: This word helps the Christian reader understand the Jewish calendar and the urgency of the events of the passion. It shows how Jesus, the Passover Lamb, was put to death precisely on the day of the "preparation" of the Passover. This detail emphasizes that everything is fulfilled according to God's plan: the timing of the crucifixion is not a coincidence, but fits within the sacred time of Israel.

sens: To extend in duration, to make last longer
To continue a discourse beyond the expected duration
G3905.detail:
1. The verb prolong means to extend something in time, to make it last longer than expected. It is the action of adding duration to what could have stopped earlier. The image is that of a rope being pulled to lengthen it: it is pulled forward (the prefix "para" suggests this idea of extension).
2. In its biblical usage, the word particularly denotes the act of continuing to speak, to prolong one's discourse. In Acts 20:7, Paul converses with the disciples and "prolongs his discourse until midnight": he speaks longer than might have been expected, as he has much to say to them before leaving.
G3905.origine: The verb comes from the Greek prefix "para" (beside, along) and the verb "teinô" (to stretch, to extend). This combination evokes the idea of extending something by pulling it alongside or forward, which prolongs its duration. The word sometimes translates the Hebrew "shaqaph" (to look down, to extend above), showing that the idea of duration and extension is fundamental.
G3905.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 20:7. Paul, visiting Troas, spends a night with the disciples. As he must leave the next day, he takes advantage of this last opportunity to converse with them. So absorbed by his teaching and his love for these brothers, he prolongs his discourse until midnight. This context shows that the verb describes a voluntary extension, motivated by the importance of the message and pastoral affection.
G3905.portee: This word invites the believer to reflect on the value of time dedicated to the Word of God and to fellowship. Paul does not hesitate to "prolong" his discourse because the spiritual nourishment of his brothers matters more than rest. It is an invitation not to count our time when it comes to serving God and edifying others.

sens: Examine someone or something closely, looking at it carefully
Watch someone with the intention of harming or trapping them
Scrupulously respect religious practices or observances (days, seasons)
G3906.detail:
1. To observe attentively means to look at someone or something carefully and with attention to examine the details. It is to look closely, often to understand what is happening. The guards in Damascus were watching the city gates vigilantly to monitor movements (Acts 9:24).

2. To observe someone can also mean to watch them with malicious intent: one seeks to trap them or find grounds to accuse them. The Pharisees were observing Jesus on the Sabbath, watching to see if he would perform a healing so they could accuse him (Mark 3:2, Luke 6:7). Luke 20:20 shows this hostile surveillance: they were watching him to set traps and deliver him to the authorities.

3. To observe can finally mean to respect or scrupulously practice certain religious observances — such as the days, months, and seasons set by the Law. This is what Paul refers to in Galatians: they were meticulously observing the holy days of the Jewish calendar (Galatians 4:10).
G3906.origine: The Greek word παρατηρέω (paratēreō) is composed of παρα (para, "beside") and τηρέω (tēreō, "to keep, observe"). The idea is thus to "keep beside," meaning to watch closely, not to take one's eyes off. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), this word translates the Hebrew זָמַם (zamam, "to meditate on a plan") and שׁמַר (shamar, "to keep"), which shows the connection between observing attentively and having intent.
G3906.emploi: This verb appears six times in the New Testament, almost always in the Gospels. In three passages (Mark 3:2, Luke 6:7, Luke 14:1), Jesus is the object of observation: the Pharisees and scribes are watching him closely, seeking to find an opportunity to accuse him — particularly if he would heal on the Sabbath in violation of the Law. The text of Luke 20:20 specifies that this surveillance is hostile: they send spies who pretend to be pious to catch his words and bring him to justice. In Acts 9:24, the context is different: it is the city gates that are being observed, a security watch. In Galatians 4:10, Paul uses the same verb to criticize the scrupulous observation of the days and seasons of the Jewish calendar, which he considers a return to legal slavery.
G3906.portee: This word reveals how surveillance can be either harmless (looking to understand, keeping watch over a city) or malicious (seeking to trap). It also shows how a religious practice — observing holy days — can become a form of legalism if it forgets that freedom in Christ surpasses observances. For the Christian reader, this word invites discernment of the intention behind the observation: are we watching to learn and follow, or to accuse and control?

sens: Attentive observation, surveillance
The act of fixing one's eyes on something
A visible or observable manner of appearing
G3907.detail:
1. The word denotes attentive observation or surveillance — the act of looking closely at something to examine it. It is to look with fixed eyes, with attention.

2. By extension, it evokes the manner in which something presents itself to the eyes, how one can perceive or notice it. In Luke 17:20, Jesus says that the kingdom of God does not come "in a way that draws attention": it does not arrive in a way that one can see coming, observe progressing, or point out saying, "Here it is" or "There it is."

3. This contrasts with visible, measurable things that can be observed and followed with the eyes — as opposed to spiritual realities that escape external observation.
G3907.origine: The word comes from the verb παρατηρέω (paratēreō), which means "to observe attentively." It is formed from παρα (para, "beside") and τηρέω (tēreō, "to keep, watch"). The initial image is that of someone standing beside something to watch it, examining it closely. The corresponding Hebrew root in the Old Testament is שׁמר (šāmar), which means "to keep, observe, watch."
G3907.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 17:20. In this verse, Jesus responds to the Pharisees who ask him when the kingdom of God will come. He explains that the kingdom does not come in a way that draws attention — meaning that it cannot be observed from the outside, pointed out, or visually followed like a political or military event. The word emphasizes that the kingdom of God is a spiritual reality, invisible to the human eye, and not a phenomenon that can be seen coming and measured objectively.
G3907.portee: This word reminds us that the kingdom of God does not manifest itself like visible and observable earthly kingdoms. Faith in Christ is not based on what can be seen, measured, or monitored from the outside, but on an inner transformation and a spiritual relationship. It encourages the Christian to seek the realities of God beyond appearances and not to reduce the presence of the Lord to what human eyes can grasp.

sens: Place something before someone, especially food at a table
Entrust something or someone to the care or responsibility of another
Put forward an argument, a word, or a teaching before an audience
G3908.detail:
1. The primary meaning is concrete: to put an object or food in front of a person. This is especially the case when serving a meal. In Mark 6:41, Jesus breaks the bread and "distributes" it to the disciples so that they can "present" it to the crowd; in Mark 8:6-7, he "distributes" the fish to the guests after giving thanks. The image is that of a server placing the dish in front of the eaters.
2. Figuratively, it means to entrust something to someone, giving them charge or responsibility. In Luke 23:46, Jesus "commits" his spirit into the hands of the Father — he entrusts it to him in full confidence at the moment of his death. Similarly, in Acts 20:32, Paul "commends" his listeners to God and to his grace, meaning he places them under his care. In 2 Timothy 2:2, Timothy must entrust to other teachers what he has learned from Paul.
3. Sometimes, the word means to propose, to present a teaching or a word. In Matthew 13:24 and 13:31, Jesus "presents" parables to his disciples, putting them "before" them so they can listen and learn.
G3908.origine: The Greek word παρατίθημι (paratithēmi) is composed of παρά (para, "beside") and τίθημι (tithēmi, "to place, to put"). The basic image is thus: to place something "beside" someone, to "put it before". In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew שׂוּם (sum), which means "to place, establish, put." The preposition παρά gives the verb a nuance of intimacy or closeness: one does not place something from afar, but near the person, before their eyes.
G3908.emploi: The word appears 18 times in the New Testament. It is mainly used in the Gospels (Mark, Luke, Matthew) and the Pauline epistles (Acts, 1 Corinthians, 1 and 2 Timothy, 1 Peter). In the meal narratives — particularly the feeding of the multitudes — it describes the action of serving or distributing food (Mark 6:41, 8:6-7, Luke 9:16). In Jesus' teachings, it denotes the act of proposing a parable to the disciples (Matthew 13:24, 13:31). More often, it takes on the spiritual meaning of entrusting someone or something to a trustworthy person or to God himself — this is the dominant meaning when Paul entrusts the churches to God or when Timothy must pass on the teaching to others (2 Timothy 2:2, Acts 20:32).
G3908.portee: This word speaks to the Christian of two important realities. First, it reminds us that Jesus "presents" the divine word in a simple and concrete manner, like placing bread on the table: God's teaching is not inaccessible; it is offered nearby, within reach of the listener. Secondly, it invites trust: when one "commits" something or someone to God, one acknowledges that they do not keep it for themselves, but place it in safe hands. This is the attitude of the dying Jesus who "commits" his spirit to the Father, and that of the believer who "commends" their life to God.

sens: To find oneself by chance in the presence of someone
To cross paths with someone, to be where they arrive
G3909.detail:
1. The word conveys the idea of being there, by chance or circumstance, when someone passes by. It is an unplanned encounter, a fortuitous presence. In Acts 17:17, Paul "meets" different people every day in the marketplace — they arrive, he is there, the meeting happens naturally.

2. It also simply refers to being present, available to talk or interact with someone. Paul goes to the synagogue and the marketplace with the intention of discussing with those he encounters, showing that "to meet" here means to be in the presence of someone and to speak to them.
G3909.origine: The word combines two elements: the prefix παρα- ("beside," "near") and τυγχάνω ("to happen, to occur by chance"). The image is one of being nearby when something or someone arrives. It is a verb of simple presence or fortuitous occurrence, quite rare in the New Testament.
G3909.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Acts 17:17, when Paul dialogues in Athens. He describes himself as conversing "every day with those he met" in the marketplace. The context shows Paul as someone available, who engages in conversation with all those who cross his path — Jews, God-fearing Gentiles, or other residents. It is a simple active presence open to meeting.
G3909.portee: This word reminds us that sharing the Gospel does not require complex organization: Paul seizes every encounter, every chance conversation as an opportunity to witness. It is a lesson on availability and spiritual opportunism — knowing how to preach at every opportunity, with those whom God places in our path.

sens: Lasting for a moment, fleeting
Having little weight, of little importance
G3910.detail:
1. The word describes what lasts only a moment, what is fleeting and temporary. Paul uses it in 2 Corinthians 4:17 to qualify present afflictions: they seem overwhelming at the moment, but in the scale of eternity, they are merely temporary. The adverb emphasizes the contrast between the brevity of these sufferings and the eternal glory that will result from them.
2. By extension, the word designates what is lightweight, without lasting significance. Called "light," these afflictions are not without reality (they are indeed present), but they lose their heaviness when related to God and His work. It is a matter of perspective: what seems overwhelming becomes bearable and even productive when viewed in relation to God's promises.
G3910.origine: The word comes from the root meaning "beside" (παρά) and "itself, same" (αὐτά), forming the idea of an action "at the very moment" or "right away." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the equivalent can be found in words expressing immediacy or brevity. This adverbial construction, well attested in classical Greek, emphasizes the transient and momentary nature of what is described.
G3910.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 4:17. Paul chooses it to express a deep spiritual conviction: the tribulations that the apostles endure are real and present, but they are brief compared to the eternal reward. The adjective "light" does not deny suffering, but places it in the perspective of God and eternity. It is a pastoral word, intended to encourage believers in trials by reminding them that the present time is not the final word.
G3910.portee: For the believer, this word offers a liberating perspective: the difficulties of today, no matter how heavy they may be, are not definitive. They last "for a moment" in the scale of eternity. Paul invites us to see the present life not as the ultimate horizon, but as a brief moment in God's plan. This word comforts those who suffer by reminding them that the duration of the trial is limited and that its end will lead to an incomparable glory.

sens: To take away, to distance something from someone or oneself
To divert someone from a direction, doctrine, or belief
To be carried away, deviated from one's true nature
G3911.detail:
1. The primary and most concrete meaning is to physically remove something: to take away or distance an object. In Jesus' prayers at Gethsemane (Mark 14:36 and Luke 22:42), this is exactly the meaning: Jesus asks His Father to remove the cup of suffering from Him, just as one would push away an undesirable object.

2. Figuratively, the word means to divert someone from their path or lead them away from the truth. In Hebrews 13:9, Paul warns: "Do not be led away by diverse and strange doctrines." Here, the word describes a spiritual distancing, a deviation from sound doctrine by deceptive influences.

3. In the passive voice, the word can also mean to be carried away or led astray oneself: one is pushed away from the right direction, like a leaf carried by the wind. This idea appears in Jude 12, where the image is of a person led astray.
G3911.origine: The word is composed of para ("beside, away from") and pherō ("to carry, to take away"). The basic image is therefore one of carrying something aside, that is, to remove or distance it. This composition suggests a movement that departs from the normal position: one carries away, one deviates. The Hebrew root halal (to praise) in 1 Kings 21:13 translated by this Greek verb in the Old Testament shows how the same action can be perceived differently depending on the context: what is supposed to be a praise becomes a deviation.
G3911.emploi: The verb paraferō appears four times in the New Testament preserved for us. Its two most famous uses are found in the accounts of the agony at Gethsemane (Mark 14:36 and Luke 22:42), where Jesus asks the Father to remove the cup of His suffering. In Hebrews 13:9, the word is in the passive imperative and means "do not be led away": there is the idea of an external force that could lead us away from sound doctrine. In Jude 12, used in the past tense, it describes men who have been led away from the right path. The verb therefore designates either a voluntary physical separation (asking for removal) or a spiritual deviation that is suffered or ignored.
G3911.portee: This word speaks to every Christian who knows the temptation to stray from the received truth. It reminds us that vigilance is necessary: the Hebrew verb "to lead away" shows us that one does not need to deliberately choose error; it is enough to be "carried" away without being aware of it. At the same time, Jesus' prayer at Gethsemane shows that entrusting to God what weighs us down (by asking for removal) is an act of faith and submission: we ask God to remove from us what exceeds our strength.

G3912.fr: to be out of one's mind
sens: To lose reason, to be disturbed in mind
To be excessive, to exceed the limits of moderation
To act in a foolish manner or against the normal order of things
G3912.detail:
1. The primary meaning of the word is literal: to lose the normal use of reason, to be in a troubled or disturbed mental state. It is the image of a person who is no longer in control of their mind, who has lost the ability to think clearly.

2. By extension, the word also expresses the idea of exceeding the measure, of acting with an excess that goes beyond common limits. In 2 Corinthians 11:23, the Apostle Paul uses this verb to describe his extreme commitment to the service of Christ — a dedication so radical that it borders, in the eyes of the world, on a total lack of common sense.

3. More broadly, it is to act in a way that transgresses the established order, which seems foolish according to ordinary criteria. The underlying idea is one of a break with the norm, a conduct that common sense would disapprove of.
G3912.origine: The word is composed of *para* (beside, beyond) and *phroneō* (to have good sense, to think wisely) — literally "to think beside," that is, to lose the thread of ordered thought. The root *phrēn* refers to the mind, intelligence, the seat of judgment. Words of the same family (*phronesis*, *phronimos*) evoke wisdom and prudence; *paraphroneō* is its exact opposite, the negative reverse: the absence of wisdom.
G3912.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 11:23. Paul uses it in an apologetic context where he enumerates the trials and dangers he has endured for Christ: persecutions, stonings, shipwrecks. When he says, "I speak as a madman" (*paraphroneō*), he acknowledges that his own testimony — this path of suffering for the sake of the Gospel — may seem entirely unreasonable to the world. He himself measures the apparent absurdity of his commitment, which actually adds weight to his argument: he knows he seems foolish, and he states it honestly.
G3912.portee: This word invites the reader to reconsider what true wisdom really means. What the world calls folly — radical trust in Christ, acceptance of suffering for the Gospel — may be, in God's eyes, the only true wisdom. Paul, by using this verb, reminds that the disciple of Christ must sometimes accept to appear foolish according to the world's standards, for these are not God's standards.

sens: Loss of reason, severe mental derangement
Folly that drives one to act against divine wisdom and justice
G3913.detail:
1. Madness is the loss of the ability to think clearly and to act wisely. It is a deep confusion of the mind. In the text of 2 Peter 2:16, it refers to the derangement of the prophet Balaam, who despite divine knowledge persisted in cursing Israel — a spiritual folly that was only interrupted by the miraculous intervention of the donkey.
2. Figuratively, madness characterizes one who rejects God's wisdom to follow their own desires. It is a form of moral blindness: the fool acts against the very evidence of divine truth, like Balaam who refused to obey despite the clear signs from the Lord.
G3913.origine: The word is formed from the prefix "para" (beside, beyond) and "phren" (the mind, reason). The image is that of a mind straying from the normal path, becoming disordered. The same prefix appears in other words indicating a deviation or divergence: what is "beside" the proper use becomes a defect or a disease.
G3913.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:16. Peter uses it to describe the derangement of the prophet Balaam, who coveted the wages of injustice despite God's words. The madness here is not a bodily illness, but a spiritual aberration: Balaam knew the divine will, but he denied it to satisfy his greed. That is why only a miracle — the voice of the donkey — could bring him back to reason.
G3913.portee: This word reminds us that pride and greed can mislead even a man who knows the word of God. It invites the believer to examine their heart: to follow one's own desires against the clarity of divine truth is a form of folly that only God's intervention can heal.

sens: To remain in a place during the winter season
To stay somewhere until spring
G3914.detail:
1. The verb literally means to stay or remain (hence the prefix "para") during the winter ("cheimazō"). It is a practical need: in winter, especially in the Mediterranean, maritime travel would stop. Paul writes to Titus that he plans to winter in Nicopolis (Titus 3:12), and he suggests to the Corinthians that he might winter with them (1 Corinthians 16:6) so that the community can assist him in his next journey. In Acts 28:11, we learn that a merchant ship had already wintered in Malta.
2. This word does not only describe a meteorological phenomenon: it refers to a forced stop, a waiting period. The apostles and travelers awaited the return of spring and favorable sailing conditions. That is why Paul frames his winter stay with meetings with the churches.
G3914.origine: The Greek verb "paracheimazō" is formed from the prefix "para" ("beside", "in") and "cheimazō" ("to winter"), itself derived from the noun "cheimon" (winter). It is a simple, descriptive word related to the realities of ancient life: maritime routes would close in winter, marking the rhythm of travel.
G3914.emploi: This verb appears only 4 times in the New Testament, all in contexts of apostolic travel. Paul speaks of his travel plans: he considers wintering in Nicopolis in Titus 3:12, or with the Corinthians in 1 Corinthians 16:6, which shows that these winter stays were expected and planned. In Acts 27:12 and 28:11, the word describes the situation of a merchant ship and Paul's journey to Rome: it reflects the real constraints of ancient navigation.
G3914.portee: This verb reminds us that even the apostles were subject to the realities of the physical world: the seasons, the elements, the limits of travel. This humanizes the narrative of the New Testament. But also: these winter pauses were not wasted time. They allowed the apostles to spend time with local churches, to strengthen them, to create bonds. Winter becomes a time of relationship and pastoral ministry.

sens: the action of spending the winter in a place
a pause or prolonged stop during the bad season
G3915.detail:
1. It is the action of staying in a port or place throughout the winter, waiting for the difficult season to pass. The word evokes ships that stop and do not resume their journey until spring. In Acts 27:12, Paul and his companions seek a good port to winter: a safe place where the boat and its passengers can remain protected during the winter months, when the sea is too dangerous for travel.
2. Figuratively, it refers to any prolonged halt or interruption of an activity, a time of waiting and pause. The image remains that of immobility forced by circumstances: one cannot advance, one must wait.
G3915.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "paracheimázô" (to winter beside, near) composed of "pará" (beside, near) and "cheimá" (winter, bad weather). The root "cheimá" belongs to the same family as all Greek words related to winter and bad weather. It is a common word in classical Greek to specifically designate this maritime practice: to wait out the winter in a port rather than risk the sea.
G3915.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:12, in the account of Paul's shipwreck. Luke reports that the ship carrying Paul as a prisoner to Rome needs to find a good port to winter, as it is too late in the year to continue the journey in the Mediterranean. The context shows the strategic importance of the choice: a bad port could have endangered the ship and its 276 passengers. This detail underscores the realism of the narrative and Luke's knowledge of the conditions of ancient navigation.
G3915.portee: This word reminds the reader that even in God's grand plans — here, Paul's arrival in Rome to testify — concrete realities and seasons matter. There is a time to advance and a time to wait. It also speaks of divine providence: God cares for the practical details and circumstances that surround us, even the most ordinary.

sens: The present moment, immediate, without delay
The absence of time between cause and effect, immediacy
The sudden rapidity of an action or transformation
G3916.detail:
1. The instant is that moment which arrives right away, without waiting. When Jesus curses the fig tree and "at once the fig tree withered" (Matthew 21:19), there is nothing left to wait for: the tree dies on the spot. It is the "now" that imposes itself immediately.
2. This word especially marks the absence of delay between what one does and what happens. When the fever leaves Peter's mother "at once" and she gets up (Luke 4:39), there is no interval: Jesus' command and the healing are one. It is the immediacy of divine action.
3. The instant also emphasizes the suddenness of a transformation: the blind man "at once received his sight" (Luke 18:43), the paralyzed man gets up "at that very moment" (Acts 3:7), or Herod dies "at that very moment" struck by the angel (Acts 12:23). The action is striking, without transition.
G3916.origine: The Greek word comes from the expression "παρὰ τὸ χρῆμα" ("beside what is used"), which originally referred to what was at hand, immediately available. From there came the meaning of "immediately" or "on the spot." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, similar words like "פִּתְאוֹם" (pittom, "suddenly") also mark this immediacy of action.
G3916.emploi: This word appears 19 times in the New Testament, especially in the Gospels of Luke (12 occurrences) and the account of Acts (6 occurrences), rarely in Matthew. Luke in particular uses it to show the effectiveness of Jesus' word or the Spirit: instant healings (Luke 4:39, 8:47), resurrections (Luke 8:55), conversions (Acts 9:18). Matthew uses it for the miraculous event of the fig tree withering. Acts features it when the Spirit acts manifestly or when God intervenes in judgment (death of Herod, 12:23).
G3916.portee: This word teaches us that the power of Jesus and that of the Spirit are never delayed or hindered: they act without delay. When we read "at once" in a healing or deliverance, it shows us that God is not slow and that there is no distance between His will and His action. This reinforces our confidence in His sovereignty and goodness.

sens: Spotted wild feline, powerful and feared
Animal emblematic of strength, speed, and danger in prophetic vision
G3917.detail:
1. The leopard (pardalis) is a large carnivorous feline with a spotted coat, known for its strength and ferocity. It is a formidable and admirable predator, very present in the nature of the Middle East and North Africa, which biblical authors were well acquainted with.
2. In John's vision, the leopard symbolizes power and swift movement: the beast described in Revelation 13:2 has the agile and spotted body of the leopard, emphasizing its agility and ability to act quickly and dangerously.
G3917.origine: The Greek word pardalis comes from an ancient root designating this feline animal. In Hebrew, the word נָמֵר (namer) carries the same meaning. This word belongs to the vocabulary of wild animals that the Bible mentions as symbols of power and danger; it appears in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) in the same places as the Hebrew term.
G3917.emploi: The word pardalis appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 13:2, where John describes a composite beast rising from the sea. This prophetic creature borrows characteristics from the leopard: it combines the swift and dangerous body of the leopard (pardalis) with the feet of a bear and the mouth of a lion, forming a hybrid animal that symbolizes a formidable and destructive political power. The apocalyptic context makes the leopard much more than just an animal: it is a traditional biblical emblem of malevolent strength and agility.
G3917.portee: This image of the leopard in the prophecy of Revelation invites the reader to discern the powers opposed to God in this world. Recognizing the speed and strength of the leopard in the prophetic vision reminds the Christian that evil can act with swiftness and cunning, but its destiny is judged. It is a call to vigilance and trust in Christ's ultimate victory.

sens: to be there, beside someone or something
to arrive, come to a place
to arrive at a specific moment
to be present in heart without being physically present
G3918.detail:
1. To be physically there, beside a person or a place: this is concrete presence. Paul writes to the Corinthians that absent in body, he is "present" in spirit (1 Corinthians 5:3), establishing a contrast with those who seek him in person.
2. To arrive, come to a specific place: the word describes the moment when one reaches a location. When the apostles were accused before the magistrates, it was said that they "had come" to Thessalonica (Acts 17:6).
3. To arrive at a specific moment, to intervene in time: this is a temporal presence. Jesus says that "the time" has not yet come for Him to act (John 7:6), speaking of the opportune moment.
4. To be present morally or in spirit, even when physically distant: this is an inner or moral presence. Paul assures the Corinthians that he is "present" with them through his feelings and counsel, even though they are geographically distant (2 Corinthians 10:11).
G3918.origine: The word comes from the root *par* (beside, next to) and *eimi* (to be), literally meaning "to be beside, near." It is a very ancient compound verb, forming a simple image: to be in the vicinity of someone or something. In the Greek of the Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew *bôa'* (to come, to arrive).
G3918.emploi: This verb is used 24 times in the New Testament, primarily in Paul's epistles and in Acts. In Acts, it often denotes the physical arrival or concrete presence of people (Acts 10:21, 17:6). Paul frequently uses it to refer to his presence or absence in his exchanges with the churches he founded (1 Corinthians 5:3, 2 Corinthians 10:11, 13:2), emphasizing that physical distance does not diminish his authority or spiritual responsibility. John uses it in temporal contexts (John 7:6), and Revelation in a context of divine power (Revelation 17:8). The word can also signify the imminent arrival of a moment or situation.
G3918.portee: This word reminds the Christian that there is no true absence for one who belongs to God. For Paul, his physical absence does not weaken his commitment to the churches he founded: he remains present through prayer, teaching, and spiritual vigilance. It is an encouragement not to reduce Christian fellowship to mere physical presence, but to recognize it also in the communion of spirit, prayer, and sharing of faith.

sens: To bring someone to oneself or present them
To secretly bring something in, to insinuate furtively
G3919.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to lead someone, to bring them to appear or to publicly present them — for example, presenting a guest to a group or introducing someone to an authority. It is a gesture of welcome or highlighting.

2. In the New Testament, the word takes on a shade of hidden or malevolent intention: it means to bring something in quietly, stealthily, without warning. In 2 Peter 2:1, it describes how false teachers will "introduce" destructive sects among believers — not through open preaching, but through stealthy infiltration, slipping in among the people of God to spread their error.
G3919.origine: The word is composed of three elements: *para* (beside, alongside), *eis* (to, into) and *ago* (to lead, to bring). The basic idea is therefore "to lead beside" or "to lead into." It is the classical verb for introduction or presentation. In late Greek, the addition of *para* (beside) gives the word a nuance of secrecy: to lead something "beside," in a roundabout way, rather than openly.
G3919.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:1. Peter denounces the false prophets who, as before in Israel, will bring error into the Church — not openly, but by infiltrating, "introducing" secretly doctrines contrary to Christ. The choice of this word reveals the insidious nature of false doctrine: it does not announce itself; it insinuates. It is a warning about the cunning of religious lies.
G3919.portee: This word warns the believer against the danger of deceptive teachings that sneak in without warning. It invites vigilance: one does not always spot error if it comes "softly." It is a call to examine what is taught to us, even when it comes from those who claim to speak in God's name.

sens: Who has slipped secretly into a group
Who has entered stealthily, without right or authorization
Who has infiltrated like a spy or a traitor
G3920.detail:
1. The word describes someone who has entered a place or group in a secret and deliberate manner, bypassing normal channels. In Galatians 2:4, Paul speaks of "false brothers who had secretly slipped in and mingled among us" — they mixed with the Christian assembly without being recognized for who they truly were.
2. It is an infiltration done with malevolent intent: the person seeks to deceive, to spy, or to cause harm from within. The false brothers in Galatians 2:4 aimed "to spy out the liberty we have in Christ Jesus" and to "bring us into bondage."
3. The word emphasizes the hidden and sneaky nature of the action: it is not an open arrival, but a secret penetration, like that of a spy or traitor who hides in the ranks to harm the cause from within.
G3920.origine: The word is formed from three Greek elements: "para" (beside, outside), "eis" (to, into) and "ago" (to lead, to bring). Together, they compose the idea of being brought in stealthily from the sides, outside recognized paths. It is the participle of a verb, "pareisakto," which literally means "to bring secretly to." The image is that of a clandestine entry, of smuggling in.
G3920.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Galatians 2:4. Paul uses it to describe the "false brothers" who had secretly penetrated the ranks of the Church to spy on Christian freedom and seek to enslave the faithful. It is a very loaded word: it associates secret physical infiltration with spiritual malevolence. Paul uses it to warn against dangers that threaten the Christian assembly from within — not just external opponents, but those who hide among the brethren with destructive intentions.
G3920.portee: This word reminds us that the Church is not immune to malevolent infiltrations and that vigilance is necessary. The Christian is invited to discern, not to trust blindly anyone who claims to be a believer, and to defend the authenticity of the community and the freedom that Christ has brought. It is also a call to personal sincerity: we must never seek to introduce ourselves into the life of an assembly or friendship under false pretenses or with hidden intentions.

sens: To introduce oneself furtively into a place without being noticed
To secretly penetrate a group of people
To insidiously insinuate oneself to harm or deceive
G3921.detail: 1. The word evokes the image of someone who slips, who discreetly weaves their way somewhere as if they had no right to be there. It is a furtive entry, almost invisible: one flows in, infiltrates without attracting attention. Jude uses it exactly this way when speaking of false teachers who have slipped in among Christians (Jude 1:4). 2. Figuratively, it means to insidiously penetrate a group, a community, in secret, with the intention to harm. These men do not make themselves known: they act in the shadows to corrupt the faith of believers by turning grace into licentiousness. The verb emphasizes the sneaky and dangerous nature of this intrusion.
G3921.origine: The word is composed of three Greek elements: "para" (beside, among), "eis" (into), and "dunô" (to plunge, to slip). This composition underscores the idea of gradually introducing oneself, without force, in a concealed manner. It is a rare word in Greek, formed to express this precise notion of secret infiltration into an environment.
G3921.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament: in Jude 1:4, where Jude denounces the false teachers who have slipped in among Christians. These are heretical teachers who have secretly penetrated the Church to corrupt it from within. The context shows that this infiltration is voluntary, premeditated, and motivated by malevolence: these men deny Christ and turn grace into permissiveness. The choice of this exact verb — rather than a simple "enter" — emphasizes the deliberate and sneaky nature of their intrusion.
G3921.portee: This word warns the Christian against the danger of seducers who operate in secret. It reminds us that faith can be infiltrated by false doctrines that present themselves under the guise of piety, but undermine the truth of the Gospel. This exhorts the believer to remain vigilant and to discern the spirits, for lies do not shout from the street corner: they slip in slowly, gradually, in deceptive softness.

sens: Arrive, enter alongside something or on the way
Enter secretly, intrude stealthily
G3922.detail:
1. The verb describes the arrival of something that comes to add to an existing situation, as one enters through a side door. In Romans 5:20, the Law "intervenes" in the history of salvation: it comes after Adam's sin, inserting itself into God's plan, like an added force that causes the offense to abound before grace surpasses it.

2. The same verb can also mean to intrude secretly, uninvited, with a hidden intention. This is the meaning in Galatians 2:4: false brothers "slipped in" among the Christians in Jerusalem, discreetly infiltrating with the secret intention of spying on Christian freedom and enslaving believers. The image is that of a disloyal intrusion.
G3922.origine: The word is composed of three Greek elements: *para* ("beside," "against"), *eis* ("into"), and *erchomai* ("to come"). Its basic etymology paints the image of a coming that inserts itself into an existing trajectory, sometimes as an external addition (the intervening Law), sometimes as a clandestine infiltration. This composition reveals the idea of an arrival "in addition to" or "outside the normal order."
G3922.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, in contexts rich in meaning for Pauline theology. In Romans 5:20, Paul describes the historical role of the Law: it was not the initial plan, but it intervened after sin to reveal the offense and, paradoxically, for grace to abound even more. In Galatians 2:4, the same verb designates the infiltration of false brothers who threaten freedom in Christ. In both uses, the verb never carries a positive connotation: something external or illegal imposes itself or attempts to impose itself.
G3922.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us of two major truths: first, that the Mosaic Law, despite its holy and just character, is not God's original intention, but a later intervention to reveal sin and prepare the way for grace. Secondly, it warns against false teachers who infiltrate the Church to pervert freedom in Christ. It is a call to remain vigilant and discern what comes from God's original plan and what imposes itself against His will.

sens: Bring in addition, provide through personal effort
Exert diligence by progressively adding to what one possesses
G3923.detail:
1. The word evokes the action of bringing something in addition, beyond what already exists. It is to add a stone to the building, to provide an extra effort. In 2 Peter 1:5, Peter urges his readers to "make every effort to add to your faith virtue" — it is about actively providing, exerting diligence to progressively add spiritual qualities to their foundational faith.
2. The word also carries the idea of personal responsibility: it is not God who passively adds these qualities, but the believer himself who must engage. The effort required implies a deliberate will of the Christian, not a mere expectation of passive grace.
G3923.origine: The word is composed of three Greek elements: "para" (beside, in addition), "eis" (toward, into), and "pherō" (to bear, to bring). This composition expresses the idea of bringing in addition. It is a relatively rare term in ancient Greek, created to speak of a dynamic action of addition or provision. The root "pherō" (to bear) is very common and appears in many Greek words expressing movement or transmission.
G3923.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 1:5. Peter uses it in a context of exhortation to spiritual growth: believers must "make" (exert effort) to add to their faith the moral and spiritual qualities that mark Christian maturity — virtue, knowledge, temperance, and others. The context shows that it is a progressive and voluntary work of the believer, not a passivity waiting for everything from God.
G3923.portee: This word reminds the Christian that spiritual growth requires personal commitment and diligence. Although God's grace is at work, Peter shows that the believer must actively "add" to his faith, intentionally developing these virtues. It is a call to responsibility: receiving Christ is a gift, but becoming mature requires effort and discipline on our part.

sens: Except for, aside from
Outside of, apart from
Without counting, independently of
G3924.detail:
1. The word indicates what is excluded or set apart: it is the exception to a general rule. In Matthew 5:32, Jesus says that divorce is prohibited "except" for infidelity — this infidelity is the only exception He allows.
2. It also marks a separation, what stands outside. In Acts 26:29, Paul wishes that his listeners become like him "except for" his chains — the chains are excluded from what he wishes for them.
3. The word can mean "without mentioning" or "independently of." In 2 Corinthians 11:28, Paul says that "without speaking" of other concerns, he bears daily the weight of all the churches — he temporarily sets aside other trials to enumerate this one.
G3924.origine: The word is composed of "para" (beside, against) and "ektos" (outside, exterior). Its starting image is that of a limit or boundary: what is "beside the outside" is what escapes the common rule, what is separated from it. The root "ektos" (outside) is also found in "ekstasis" (ecstasy, out of oneself) and "ekklesia" (assembly, those called out).
G3924.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament. In Matthew 5:32 and 19:9, it states the exception to Christ's command against divorce: infidelity. In Acts 26:29, Paul uses it to exclude the chains from his wish for his listeners. In 2 Corinthians 11:28, it indicates that other concerns are set aside before enumerating this one. It is a rare preposition or conjunction, used to construct precise statements where it is necessary to delineate an exception or mark an exclusion.
G3924.portee: This word teaches us the importance of precision: Jesus does not say "divorce is absolutely prohibited," but He states the exception. It is a reminder that God's commandments, while clear, may contain nuances; the reader must read them carefully to understand not only the rule but also its limits.

sens: military camp or organized soldier positions
a group of armed soldiers or army in formation
building or group of fortified buildings where soldiers reside
protected place where one can find safety
G3925.detail: 1. The word primarily designates a camp where the army sets up, with its tents and organization: it is the image of God's people crossing the Red Sea, protected by the camp of Israel (Hebrews 11:34 refers to the exploits of faith in the face of organized enemy armies). 2. It can also mean the army itself in its combat formation, troops arranged in battle order: a structured military force ready to act. 3. In Acts, the word refers to the fortress of Antioch (the Roman citadel of Jerusalem), where prisoners are held and soldiers reside. Paul is taken there several times to be interrogated or protected from the crowd (Acts 21:34, 37; 22:24; 23:10, 16, 32). 4. By extension, it is a refuge, a place where one is sheltered: for Paul, the fortress paradoxically becomes a place of safety in the face of the danger of the crowd.
G3925.origine: The word is composed of three elements: "para" (beside), "em" (in), and "ballō" (to throw). The basic meaning is "to throw beside," "to place between." In military Greek, it comes to designate what is "thrown" in place for battle: the camp, the army in formation. In ancient Hebrew, the corresponding word is "ma'haneh," which designates both the desert camp and an army on the move. This term evokes the idea of an organized, delimited, protected military installation.
G3925.emploi: The word appears ten times in the New Testament, mostly in Acts. In Hebrews, it describes the army of enemies crossed by faith (Hebrews 11:34) and the camp of the Israelites in the desert (Hebrews 13:11, 13: it refers to the tabernacle set up "outside the camp"). In Revelation, it refers to the camp of the nations surrounding the heavenly Jerusalem (Revelation 20:9). But the most frequent usage is in Acts, where the "fortress" is the Roman citadel where Paul is imprisoned and interrogated. It becomes the seat of the military authorities who decide his fate: it changes meaning according to the context, from a place of danger to a place of protection.
G3925.portee: For the reader, the fortress reminds us that even in moments of captivity or threat (Paul in Jerusalem), God can transform a place of confinement into a refuge. It also symbolizes how human institutions, even hostile ones, remain under God's control. It invites the Christian to see beyond appearances: what seems like a prison can also be a divine protection.

sens: Causing trouble, annoyance to someone
Imposing a burden, a troubling charge
G3926.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of causing trouble or annoyance to someone, particularly by imposing something burdensome on them. In Acts 15:19, James says that one should not "create difficulties" for the Gentiles who are turning to God: it is about not imposing on them observances of the Law that would trouble or unnecessarily burden them.
2. The word suggests the idea of a burden, a nuisance added to someone from the outside, like an added hassle (hence the prefix *para-*, "beside," "in addition"). It is to cause a disturbance, an unexpected embarrassment.
G3926.origine: The word is composed of the prefix *para-* ("beside," "in addition") and *enochléō* ("to trouble," "to inconvenience"), which comes from *ochlos* ("crowd," "trouble"). The image is that of a nuisance or disturbance imposed on someone from the outside. In Hebrew, the Old Testament Greek translates this verb *lā'â* (in the causative form), which means "to tire," "to disgust."
G3926.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 15:19. James uses it during the Jerusalem council to recommend not to burden the Gentile converts with overly heavy legal obligations. It is a word chosen to strongly express the idea that certain rules would only annoy, trouble the new believers and divert them from the essence of faith. The context shows that the apostle seeks to protect access to God by avoiding unnecessary hindrances.
G3926.portee: This word helps the reader understand the pastoral wisdom of the apostles: their concern is not to multiply rules, but to free converts from superfluous burdens. It reminds us that faith should not be hindered by artificial obstacles, and that God's grace invites simplicity rather than the weight of human demands.

sens: one who temporarily resides in a place that is not their homeland
one who has no civic rights in a place
the believer who considers the earth as a place of passage
G3927.detail:
1. A traveler is someone who lives in a place without being permanently established there, like Abraham who recognized himself as a "stranger and traveler on the earth" (Hebrews 11:13): he does not possess citizenship rights, he is just passing through.
2. The word also designates one who has no legal status in a city: they may reside there, but without the privileges of citizens. In Hebrews 11:13, this meaning aligns with the first — Abraham and the patriarchs lived as guests without established rights.
3. For the New Testament Church, this word takes on a spiritual meaning: the Christian, while living in this world, recognizes themselves as a traveler on the way to another homeland — that of heaven. Peter addresses the believers this way (1 Peter 1:1 and 2:11): although geographically settled, they are not "at home" since their true citizenship and true rest are with God.
G3927.origine: The Greek word comes from two parts: "para" (beside, next to) and "epidēmos" (inhabitant, someone who dwells in a place). Together, they form the image of a person who resides "beside" the true homeland, who is present there but does not truly belong to it — a resident without citizen status. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew "toshab," which designates the resident alien.
G3927.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, all in the epistles of Peter or in Hebrews, addressed to dispersed Christian communities. In Hebrews 11:13, it characterizes Abraham and the patriarchs who believed in God's promise without seeing it fulfilled on earth. In 1 Peter 1:1 and 2:11, Peter uses this word to remind the dispersed churches that, although living in their places of residence, they should not consider themselves as permanently established in this world: they are called to a heavenly homeland. The context is always one of tension between a present dwelling and an absent true homeland.
G3927.portee: This word invites the Christian to a perspective of healthy detachment from the present world: it exists, certainly, but without rooting oneself in it as if it were their true home. This frees one from anxiety for earthly riches and honors, and directs the heart toward heaven — which was already the faith of the patriarchs. For those who meditate on these words, it is an invitation to live here with restraint and holiness, in anticipation of eternal rest with God.

sens: To move from one place to another, to go beyond
To disappear, cease to exist
To leave aside, to intentionally neglect
To arrive before someone
G3928.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of movement: a person or thing crossing a space or moment. Jesus "passes" before his disciples on the lake (Mark 6:48); the present generation will not "pass" away before the eschatological events occur (Mark 13:30), meaning that this generation will live to see these things.

2. The most important figurative meaning is that of disappearance or end: "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away" (Matthew 24:35). Everything that is earthly and temporary "passes," fades away, ceases to be. This includes the old commandments of the Law, which will only "pass" when all is accomplished (Matthew 5:18).

3. The word can also mean to ignore or despise something: the Pharisees "pass" over justice and the love of God, meaning they neglect them (Luke 11:42). This is to overlook what truly matters.

4. Rarely, "pass" means to approach, to present oneself before someone: the master who "will come near" to his servants to serve them (Luke 12:37).
G3928.origine: The Greek verb ἐρχομαι (erkomai) means "to go, to come." The prefix παρά (para) adds the idea of "beside, near, beyond." Together, παρέρχομαι literally means "to go near" or "to pass by." In Hebrew, this verb often translates עָבַר (avar), which has the same semantic field: to pass, to cross, to exceed, but also to disappear or transgress. This etymology explains why the word covers both physical movement and the idea of passage or disappearance.
G3928.emploi: This verb appears 26 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Synoptic Gospels. In miracle accounts (Mark 6:48) and encounters (Luke 18:37), it describes simple movement. But its major theological use concerns the end of things: Jesus asserts that "heaven and earth will pass away" (Matthew 24:35; Mark 13:31; Luke 21:33), while his word remains eternal. The Law of Moses will "pass" only once all is accomplished (Matthew 5:18). In Luke 11:42 and 15:29, the verb takes on a moral shade: neglecting justice or an obligation to a parent. In 2 Corinthians 5:17, "the old man" has "passed away," annihilated by the new creation in Christ.
G3928.portee: This word teaches Christians that everything temporal and carnal "passes," while the Word of God endures forever. It invites us not to cling to this fading world, but to seek what lasts. It also calls for moral vigilance: not to "pass" over justice, love, and obedience. Finally, it proclaims that the coming of Christ ends the old economy and inaugurates a new creation.

sens: the act of not punishing a fault
forgiveness granted for a transgression
voluntary forgetting of an offense
G3929.detail:
1. It is the act of letting a fault pass without punishment, allowing it to go without chastisement. The word evokes someone who could have sanctioned but decides to turn a blind eye: this is what Paul refers to in Romans 3:25, when he says that God "let go unpunished" the sins committed before the coming of Christ.
2. By extension, it is a kind of forgiveness or remission of debt — not a complete abolition (like the related word "remission"), but rather a tolerance, a deliberate silence. God could have demanded immediate payment; he deferred it.
3. It is also the idea of a transgression forgotten or willfully ignored: not responding to it, not taking it into account in judgment.
G3929.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to let pass" or "to neglect" (παρίημι): "para" (beside) and "hiemi" (to send, to let go). The same family is found in the word "remission" (Greek ἄφεσις), which also means forgiveness or release, but through a different path. The basic image is that of something that is allowed to pass, not retained, allowed to escape.
G3929.emploi: The word appears only once in Romans 3:25, a crucial verse on justification. Paul uses it to describe God's attitude toward sins committed before Christ: the Lord did not immediately punish them, but "let them go unpunished" — not out of indifference, but as part of his redemptive plan through the blood of Christ. It is one of the few Greek words in the New Testament that carries this precise meaning of "provisional tolerance" in the face of fault.
G3929.portee: This word reminds us that God's patience, before Christ, was not an absence of judgment, but a meaningful waiting. The sins of the world did not go unanswered; God bore them within himself until the cross. For the believer, this means that every sin — including our own — has ultimately been settled at the cross, not ignored, but fully satisfied by Christ.

sens: to give, to procure, to make available
to grant, to bestow a right or a good
to cause, to produce, to occasion
to testify, to show, to manifest
to trouble, to cause repeated annoyance
to present, to offer oneself
G3930.detail:
1. The main meaning is to give or to make available: to provide something to someone. In Acts 17:31, God has "given" everyone a certain proof of the resurrection; he has made this proof available to them.
2. To grant means to consent to give, to recognize a right or to fulfill a request. In Luke 7:4, the centurion deserves "that you grant him this" — it is asking the Lord to consent to heal his servant.
3. To cause or produce means to be the source of a consequence: what is provided brings about a result. In Mark 14:6, the woman has "done" a good deed, meaning she has performed an act that produces good.
4. To testify or manifest is used to show a feeling, an attitude. In Acts 28:2, the inhabitants "testified" to us their kindness: they showed, manifested their goodness.
5. To trouble means to cause repeated annoyance, to disturb constantly. In Luke 18:5, the widow "troubles" me — she constantly comes to disturb me to obtain justice.
6. To present oneself means to voluntarily offer one's help or oneself. In Titus 2:7, the servant of God "presents" himself as a model — he offers himself as an example.
G3930.origine: The word comes from the preposition "para" (beside, towards) and the verb "echô" (to hold, to have). The basic image is therefore "to hold beside" or "to make available," hence "to provide." It is a compound verb that plays on the idea of making accessible. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates Hebrew roots meaning "to stand," "to subsist," or "to give," depending on the context.
G3930.emploi: This Greek verb appears 16 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and Epistles. It is used in the sense of "to provide, to give" when it comes to supplying material or immaterial goods (food, justice, proof). It takes on the nuance of "to show, to testify" when the complement denotes a feeling or attitude (kindness, fairness). It can also mean "to cause" when the result produced by the action is highlighted. Finally, it expresses annoyance when an action recurs incessantly, becoming tiresome. The context determines which of these meanings prevails: often it is the object of the verb (a good, a feeling, a proof) that guides the meaning.
G3930.portee: This word reminds us that God constantly "provides" for his creatures — proof of resurrection, justice, mercy. For the Christian, it invites us to become those who also provide, who give generously. It also shows us that our actions produce something, that they are not in vain: it is an encouragement to do good. Finally, the word teaches us that our prayer is not in vain when it is persistent, for it "matters" to God — he listens to it.

sens: Comfort given to someone who is suffering or sad
Word or presence that alleviates pain
Moral support and encouragement
G3931.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the concrete comfort provided to someone in distress: a gentle word, a loving presence that softens suffering. In Colossians 4:11, Paul refers to his coworkers as "a consolation," meaning that their presence and work alongside him ease his pains and support him.
2. It also signifies encouragement and exhortation that uplift morale: it is speaking to someone to restore their courage and confidence in the face of trials.
3. More broadly, it encompasses all moral or spiritual help that strengthens the heart: the presence of faithful friends, support in God's work, or the assurance that the Lord does not abandon us.
G3931.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to address, exhort, comfort." It is composed of a preposition meaning "beside" and a verb meaning "to lead" or "to guide": the idea is of someone coming alongside the one who suffers to support them. The corresponding verb (parégoreô) and the noun "consolation" appear in ancient Greek texts to describe the exhortation and comfort given in difficult times.
G3931.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Colossians 4:11. Paul uses it to describe his fellow workers in the Gospel: by working with him in the kingdom of God, despite the opposition and suffering of the apostolic ministry, they have become a true consolation for him. This choice of word emphasizes that consolation in the Christian life is not an absence of pain, but a faithful presence and sharing of the burden with other believers who walk in faith.
G3931.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that we do not bear our sufferings alone: God gives us brothers and sisters to support us, and we are called to be a consolation to one another. Consolation is not a weakness, but an act of love and courage that strengthens those who are shaken in their faith and ministry.

sens: State of one who has never had marital relations
Physical and moral purity before marriage
Consecration to God in celibacy
G3932.detail:
1. Virginity primarily refers to the state of one who has never had intimate relations with a man. It is a physical fact and a condition of life. Anna, the prophetess in Luke 2:36, "had lived seven years with her husband since her virginity" — meaning she had maintained this state until her marriage, then lived married for seven years before becoming a widow.
2. The word also evokes purity — not only physical but moral — which characterizes one who keeps themselves entirely for God or for marriage. It is a form of integrity and fidelity.
3. From a biblical perspective, virginity can express a particular consecration to God: remaining single by religious choice to devote oneself entirely to divine service, as suggested by Anna's devout life context.
G3932.origine: The word comes from the adjective "parthénos" (virgin, young woman) and the suffix "-ia" which forms abstract nouns designating a quality or state. The root points to the idea of youth and purity. In the Greek Old Testament, the same word translates the Hebrew "נְאוּר" (ne'ur, youth) in Jeremiah 3:4, showing that virginity is closely linked to youth and innocence.
G3932.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 2:36, applied to Anna. It is used to specify that she had lived single or a virgin during her youth before marrying her husband. The use of the word in connection with Anna suggests that virginity, in the biblical context, is not merely a transient state but a significant reality in the life of a pious woman. Anna, having remained a widow for a long time and staying at the temple in prayer and fasting, embodies a life devoted to God — her past as a virgin and her present widowhood frame a life consecrated.
G3932.portee: This word reminds us that purity and moral integrity are important biblical values. For Anna, virginity is not presented as an unattainable ideal, but as a fact of her life that contributed to her overall holiness. It also shows that the New Testament recognizes various forms of consecrated life: honorable marriage, faithful widowhood, and implicitly celibacy dedicated to God.

sens: young woman who has not had sexual relations
state of purity and chastity
person consecrated to God without marital ties
G3933.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a young woman who has never had sexual relations with a man. It is a physical and factual state: Mary is described as "a virgin betrothed to a man of the house of David, named Joseph" (Luke 1:27), highlighting her inexperience with marriage at the time of the Annunciation. The most famous example is that of Jesus, whose mother remains a virgin at his conception.
2. The word then takes on a moral and spiritual significance: virginity becomes a sign of purity, of chastity desired and maintained. Paul speaks of "virgins" in 1 Corinthians 7:34 as those who are concerned "about the things of the Lord, that they may be holy in body and spirit," suggesting that this status reflects a voluntary consecration to God rather than a mere absence of experience.
3. Finally, the word can qualify anyone who preserves moral integrity — men or women. In Revelation 14:4, the 144,000 are described as "virgins" who "have not defiled themselves": the word applies here to men, marking total spiritual and moral purity.
G3933.origine: The Greek parthenos comes from an Indo-European root evoking separation or preservation. In Hebrew, the word most often translates בְּתוּלָה (bethulah, young woman or virgin), but also עַלְמָה (alma, young woman) and נַעֲרָה (na'arah, young girl). These Hebrew terms initially had a concrete meaning (age or status) before taking on a religious and prophetic dimension, notably in Isaiah 7:14 where the "virgin" will bear a son. The Greek word has preserved and amplified this symbolic charge.
G3933.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew, Luke, and Paul. Matthew 1:23 applies it to Mary through a quotation from Isaiah, establishing the Christian doctrine of Mary's virginity. The parable of the ten virgins (Matthew 25:1-13) describes young girls waiting for the bridegroom, an image of the Church awaiting the return of Christ. Paul dedicates a section of his first letter to the Corinthians (chapters 7) to the question of virgins and marriage, where the word designates unmarried women and men who remain single by choice or necessity. In Revelation 14:4, the word applies to a spiritual elite, emphasizing that virginity here is a symbol of total separation from evil and consecration to the Lamb. The usage thus varies: concrete (civil status), moral (purity), and prophetic (eschatological expectation).
G3933.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on what purity and consecration mean in the Christian life. Mary's virginity affirms that Jesus is truly the Son of God, whom no man has fathered. For believers, the word reminds us that chastity and moral integrity are precious Christian values, not out of disdain for the body or marriage, but out of love for God and His holiness. The image of the Church as a "virgin" presented to Christ suggests that faithfulness to God is at the heart of the identity of God's people.

sens: inhabitant of Parthia, ancient empire of Asia
G3934.detail: The Parthians are the inhabitants of Parthia, a vast empire located in Asia, east of Mesopotamia. This people, formidable warriors, occupied the territory that stretched from the Tigris to the Indus, roughly corresponding to present-day Iran. On the day of Pentecost, Peter lists the peoples who came to Jerusalem for the feast, including the Parthians among the listeners of the Gospel message (Acts 2:9).
G3934.origine: The Greek word « Parthos » designates the inhabitants of Parthia (Parthia in Latin), a kingdom founded around 248 B.C. that became one of the greatest powers of the ancient world, a major rival of the Roman Empire. The name comes from the historical region of Parthia in Western Asia.
G3934.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 2:9, where it refers to the Parthians among the cosmopolitan crowd gathered in Jerusalem during Pentecost. This unique mention testifies to the geographical extent of the Jewish diaspora and the reach of the Jewish presence to the borders of the Parthian Empire, one of the two great empires of the ancient world alongside Rome.
G3934.portee: The presence of the Parthians at Pentecost underscores the universal scope of the Gospel: the Holy Spirit is communicated to people from all nations, including distant and powerful lands. This shows that the nascent Church from its origins transcends the borders of Israel and addresses all the peoples of the earth.

sens: Let pass, disregard, not take into account
Loosen, weaken, let fall loosely
Be weakened, exhausted, without strength
G3935.detail:
1. The word primarily means to leave something aside or not pay attention to it — as if letting it slip without holding onto it. In Luke 11:42, Jesus reproaches the Pharisees for neglecting justice and the love of God: they let them pass, released in their spiritual priority.
