2. In a physical sense, "release" means to loosen, to relax — as one releases the tension of a rope or muscle. It can also mean to weaken, to let fall.
3. When speaking of a person, it describes the state of someone whose strength is released, relaxed, extinguished. In Hebrews 12:12, the "drooping hands" are released, limp hands, without energy — the image invites to "strengthen" them, to lift them up, to straighten them.
G3935.origine: The word combines the prefix παρ- ("beside," "beyond") and the verb ἵημι ("to send, to throw"). The basic image is "to let go beside oneself, not to hold back." In Hebrew, there are related words that express this idea of relaxation and weakening, particularly the image of the release of strength or attention.
G3935.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament (Hebrews 12:12). The context is one of exhortation to perseverance: believers fatigued by suffering and divine discipline are invited not to let their hands be "released" (weakened), but to strengthen them. The word paints a spiritual and moral reality — that of weariness, abandonment, discouragement — and the call to regain strength, to straighten up in faith.
G3935.portee: This word speaks to the heart of one who is going through trial. It acknowledges that spiritual fatigue is real: hands become limp, knees weaken. But Scripture does not accept capitulation. It calls the believer to lift up what has been released, to regain strength and vigilance in the hand of God. It is a call to recovery, to the resurrection of the spirit.

sens: Put before someone, offer, deliver
Stand beside someone, be present
Appear, show oneself
Come, arrive, be there
Assist someone, help them
G3936.detail:
1. To put before someone something or someone: to hand over, offer, physically deliver. Jesus says that he can call his Father who would "immediately" give him more than twelve legions of angels (Matthew 26:53). Paul exhorts believers to "present" their members as slaves to righteousness instead of impurity (Romans 6:19). The apostle rejoices in having betrothed the Corinthians to Christ to "present" them to him as a pure virgin (2 Corinthians 11:2).
2. To stand beside someone, to be physically near them. Men were "near" Paul and the high priest when he compared him to the scribes (Acts 23:4). The centurion was "in front of" Jesus at the moment of his death (Mark 15:39). This is the image of immediate presence, of proximity.
3. To appear, to show oneself to someone, to occur visibly and suddenly. Two men dressed in white "appeared" to the disciples who were watching Jesus ascend to heaven (Acts 1:10). This is a notable, remarkable appearance.
4. To be there, to be present, to have arrived at a given moment. When the harvest is ripe, it "is there" (Mark 4:29). A servant stands "in the presence of God" (Luke 1:19). The meaning emphasizes presence or availability at a crucial moment.
5. To assist someone, to help them, to defend them, to be useful to them in a difficult moment. The Lord "stood by" Paul and strengthened him during his trials (2 Timothy 4:17). This is active help, solidarity.
G3936.origine: The word comes from "par" (beside) and a verb that means to stand or place. Its basic image is "to place beside," hence "to stand near" or "to put before." It often translates the Hebrew עָמַד (amad), which literally means to stand. This root produces in Greek a range of meanings: from the most concrete and physical (standing beside) to the more abstract and moral (presenting someone to God, offering one's life). The word family also includes "presence" and "assistance."
G3936.emploi: This verb appears about forty times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Pauline epistles. In the sense of "present" or "offer," it is found in moral exhortation (Romans 6, 12; 2 Corinthians 11:2; Colossians 1:22): presenting one's members, life, body to God or to righteousness. In the sense of "standing beside" or "being present," it describes a physical presence, such as at the foot of the cross (Mark 15:39; John 19:26) or during an angelic appearance (Acts 1:10). The sense of "assisting" or "helping" appears mainly in Paul (Romans 16:2; 2 Timothy 4:17) to express help in trials. The usage is flexible: the same verb can mean to put before, to hand over, to appear, or to stand beside depending on the context and voice (active or passive).
G3936.portee: This word reveals how the Bible conceives our relationship with God and others. Presenting one's life to God means truly handing over, offering without reservation what we are. The image of standing beside someone to help enriches our understanding of the Holy Spirit and Christian solidarity: the Lord is present to assist us, and we are called to assist our brothers and sisters. It is a word of mutual commitment and trust deposit.

sens: One of the seven men chosen to serve in the distribution to the widows of the early Church
G3937.detail: Parmenas is a man elected from among the seven first deacons of the Church in Jerusalem. After Pentecost, the Church was growing so rapidly that the apostles could not attend to all the material needs of the believers, particularly the widows. The apostles therefore entrusted seven men recognized for their faith and wisdom with the task of distributing aid fairly (Acts 6:5).
G3937.origine: The Greek name Parmenās (Παρμενᾶς) literally means "the one who perseveres" or "the persevering one," formed from the root that expresses constancy and firmness. It is a Greek name borne by this Hellenistic deacon, a member of the Greek community in Jerusalem.
G3937.emploi: Parmenas appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 6:5, where he is listed among the seven men chosen to serve tables. His name appears in a prestigious list alongside Stephen (who becomes the first martyr) and Philip (who will become an evangelist). This group of seven men marks a crucial turning point in the organization of the early Church: it is the moment when the office of deacons is born, a role intended to free the apostles for prayer and teaching.
G3937.portee: The choice of Parmenas reminds us that every Christian, whether obscure or well-known, has a place and a function in the body of Christ. Although we know little else about his life, his presence among the seven deacons shows that the humble service of meeting the concrete needs of others is a work honored by the Church. It is an invitation not to despise the practical tasks of community service.

sens: Action of moving from one place to another
Fact of crossing a place without stopping
G3938.detail:
1. The action of moving from one place to another: it is the simple movement of crossing a space. The word paints the image of a traveler crossing a region.

2. The fact of crossing a place without stopping, in passing: it is to pass quickly, in an ephemeral manner. In 1 Corinthians 16:7, Paul writes that he does not want to see them simply "in passing" (ἐν παρόδῳ), but to stay with them for a long time — he thus contrasts the quick and superficial passing with a substantial visit.
G3938.origine: The word comes from the Greek preposition πάρα (para, "beside, along") and the verb ὁδός (hodos, "way"). The image is that of movement along the way. In Hebrew, this meaning is found in דֶּרֶךְ (derek, "way, path"), which Greek sometimes translates with this word. The root speaks of movement in space, the passage from one point to another.
G3938.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 16:7. Paul announces that he does not want to see the Corinthians simply "in passing" during a journey, but to remain there for a long time if God permits. It is a concrete and practical usage: Paul refuses the quick visit and favors a lasting presence with the church.
G3938.portee: This word reminds Christians of the importance of real and engaged presence. A relationship, a ministry, a visit is not limited to superficial passing: it is the duration, commitment, and availability that build brotherly communion. For an apostle like Paul, staying with the churches rather than "passing" was a fundamental pastoral act.

sens: To live temporarily in a place
To dwell as a stranger among a population that is not one's own
To live in a region without being truly from there
G3939.detail: 1. The verb παροικέω describes the act of living in a place, but temporarily or provisionally, without the intention of settling there permanently. This is how the disciples ask Jesus if he is really "the only one who stays in Jerusalem" (Luke 24:18), giving the impression that he is just lodging there for a while. 2. The word also carries the idea of being a stranger in the place where one lives: one lives there without truly belonging, without having roots. Abraham "settled in the promised land as in a foreign land, living in tents" (Hebrews 11:9): he had received the promise of the land, but he lived there as a nomad, aware that he was just a visitor, a passing stranger. 3. The general meaning is to dwell somewhere as a stranger to that place — neither master nor truly at home.
G3939.origine: The word is composed of παρά ("beside, near") and οἰκέω ("to dwell"). The starting image is that of staying beside, like a neighbor or an outsider. In Hebrew and Aramaic, it primarily translates גּוּר ("to sojourn as a stranger"), the root word for the immigrant who has no land. This family of words emphasizes the biblical idea of God's people as strangers and travelers on earth.
G3939.emploi: The verb appears twice in the New Testament. In Luke 24:18, a disciple uses it to say that Jesus seems only to be passing through Jerusalem. In Hebrews 11:9, it characterizes Abraham's life in the promised land: although he had received the promise, he lived there as a stranger, in tents, showing his faith in a reality deeper than earthly possession. In both cases, the word evokes a presence that is not rooted, a life in transit.
G3939.portee: This word reminds Christians that faith also means accepting to be a stranger on earth. Abraham, despite God's promise, chose to live as a nomad rather than settle as a master: this attitude expresses a confident expectation of heavenly promises rather than an appropriation of the present world. For those who read the Bible, it is an invitation not to root too deeply in a world that passes away.

sens: The act of dwelling temporarily in a place, away from one's country of origin
The state of one who lives as a stranger, not being from the country
A period of life spent away from home, in exile or pilgrimage
G3940.detail:
1. The stay is the act of dwelling for a certain time in a foreign place, like the Israelites who lived in Egypt before returning to Canaan (Acts 13:17: "He honored this people during their stay in the land of Egypt"). It is a limited time away from home.
2. The word also designates the condition of the stranger or the pilgrim: one who lives somewhere without really being from that place, always a bit out of place, a bit outside. In 1 Peter 1:17, the apostle calls Christians to live in fear "during the time of your pilgrimage": earthly life is a temporary stay, one is not really from anywhere, one is just passing through.
G3940.origine: The word comes from the Greek παρά (para, "beside") and οἰκία (oikia, "dwelling"). The image is that of living "beside," that is, with others, without being at home. It shares the same root as παροικέω (paroikeô, "to dwell as a stranger"). The Hebrew גּוֹלָה (gôlâ, "exile, captivity") and מָגוֹר (mâgôr, "stay away from home") express the equivalent in the Old Testament.
G3940.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Acts 13:17, Paul remembers the stay of the Israelites in Egypt, an important phase of their history before the exodus and return to Canaan: this stay has a duration, an end. In 1 Peter 1:17, the context is less historical than spiritual: Peter affirms to the dispersed Christians that their life here is a pilgrimage, a temporary stay. The word takes on a moral and theological value: the believer must not forget that he does not belong to this world, he is passing through.
G3940.portee: This word invites the believer to relativize his attachment to earthly things. Like Abraham, who lived as a pilgrim, the Christian is called to recognize that his true home is in heaven. This awareness of the temporary stay should free one from the anxiety of judgment and inspire a life of respect toward God: one is only passing through, so one should live in a manner worthy and conscious of this condition.

sens: a person who resides in a place without being a citizen, a temporary inhabitant
a person without citizenship rights, excluded from the political community
one who does not belong to a people, a family, a household
a figure of the believer's condition on earth: a traveler far from their true homeland
G3941.detail:
1. In the literal sense, it refers to someone who lives in a country without having the rights of a citizen: they reside there but are not rooted in it. Abraham and his descendants are foreigners in Egypt who will "sojourn" there for four hundred years (Acts 7:6); Moses flees Egypt and "sojourns" in Midian (Acts 7:29) — he lives there, but does not truly belong to that place.
2. It also refers to one who does not have access to the city, to civic rights: you are no longer "outside," outside the common household (Ephesians 2:19).
3. In a figurative and spiritual sense, the term describes the believer in this world: you are "foreigners" and travelers here below (1 Peter 2:11), which means that the Christian should not set their heart on present things.
G3941.origine: The Greek word comes from pará (beside, near) and oikos (house, dwelling): literally "one who dwells beside," that is, outside the house, on the margins. It translates the Hebrew gêr (resident foreigner) and tôshab (resident alien). The basic image is one of non-rootedness: one is physically somewhere, but does not fully belong there.
G3941.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament. In Acts, it designates the concrete state of the patriarchs and Moses: they actually dwell in foreign lands. In Paul (Ephesians 2:19), it loses its purely legal sense to become a figure of communion: the Gentiles are no longer foreigners in relation to the Church. In Peter (1 Peter 2:11), it completely shifts to the figurative: the believer is a "foreigner" on earth because their true citizenship is in heaven. This evolution shows how the Bible transposes the idea: from a concrete political status to the spiritual status of a disciple of Jesus.
G3941.portee: This word reminds the believer that they should not feel completely at home in this world. Like Abraham who awaited the city with eternal foundations, the Christian is a passerby here below — which calls them not to cling to temporal riches and pleasures. It is both a warning (guard against desires) and a promise (you have a true homeland elsewhere).

sens: An enigmatic or veiled word that requires explanation
A saying or popular wisdom expressed in a striking manner
An illustrative story that teaches a deep truth by comparison
G3942.detail:
1. In the broadest sense, παροιμία refers to a word "in passing" that is not clear at first glance: it wraps its meaning in an enigmatic or figurative form. Jesus tells his disciples in John 10:6 that he spoke to them "in parables," and "they did not understand what he was saying" — the word refers to this veiled language that hides the true meaning.
2. It is also a transmitted wisdom, a memorable saying due to its striking formulation. In 2 Peter 2:22, the apostle quotes an ancient "proverb" ("The dog returns to what it has vomited"): it is a popular maxim, a saying that has circulated for a long time because it was found to be true and well said.
3. In the Gospels of John especially, the word designates Jesus' figurative language — his stories and figurative teachings that convey a divine truth using scenes from the visible world. In John 16:25 and 16:29, Jesus promises a day when he will speak "openly" and no longer "in parables": at that moment, he will reveal the Father directly without needing images.
G3942.origine: The Greek word παροιμία comes from παρά ("beside," "next to") and ὁδός ("way") — literally a word "beside the way," a word of everyday life that one hears in passing. It is an expression sanctified by popular usage. In biblical Hebrew, the same role is played by מָשַׁל (mashàl), which in Isaiah 14:4 and elsewhere designates a saying, an allegory, or an enigmatic formula. In the Septuagint (ancient translation), παροιμία regularly translates this Hebrew term.
G3942.emploi: The word παροιμία appears 4 times in the New Testament: 3 times in John (10:6, 16:25, 16:29) and once in 2 Peter 2:22. John uses it to describe the veiled manner in which Jesus teaches; it is a very characteristic trait of the fourth Gospel, where the Master speaks "in riddles" that the listeners do not grasp at first. In 2 Peter 2:22, it is an ancient word, a proverbial saying cited for its moral truth. In both cases (John and 2 Peter), the word carries the idea of a hidden meaning or a transmitted formula, but in John it is particularly enigmatic, while in 2 Peter it is more of a recognized maxim.
G3942.portee: This word reminds the reader that Jesus often speaks in a veiled manner — his parables do not reveal their meaning on the surface; they require listening and discernment. Understanding a παροιμία means accepting to dig beyond the words, allowing the image and metaphor to instruct us. It invites the Christian not to settle for a superficial reading of Scripture but to seek the deep meaning that God has hidden for those who have ears to hear.

sens: Who drinks wine excessively and habitually
Who is dominated by wine
Whose character is marked by alcoholic intemperance
G3943.detail:
1. The word literally designates someone who spends a lot of time with wine, who drinks it regularly and without moderation. It is a character trait, a rooted habit: in 1 Timothy 3:3, the apostle Paul requires that the overseer not be "given to wine," meaning that they should not be enslaved by this passion.

2. Beyond simple excessive consumption, the word evokes a loss of self-control: the person addicted to wine allows this substance to control them, compromising their judgment and dignity. In Titus 1:7, the requirement is the same for the overseer: their spiritual authority rests on sobriety and clarity of mind.
G3943.origine: The Greek word combines two elements: "para" (beside, with) and "oinos" (wine). The image is that of someone who lives beside wine, who is its constant companion. It is an adjective from Koine Greek, formed to describe a persistent character trait. The word belongs to the vocabulary family of wine in the New Testament, which also includes forms like "methé" (drunkenness) and "oinopotes" (wine drinker).
G3943.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament: in 1 Timothy 3:3 and Titus 1:7, two parallel lists of qualities required for an overseer. In both cases, Paul enumerates the faults from which one must be exempt to access this pastoral responsibility. Addiction to wine figures alongside violence, arrogance, and dishonesty — vices that disqualify a man from ministry. Paul does not condemn wine itself, but the enslavement to it, which weakens discernment and spiritual wisdom.
G3943.portee: For today's believer, this word reminds us that sobriety of spirit is inseparable from Christian maturity and pastoral responsibility. The apostle Paul establishes a clear link: one who wants to serve Christ and the Church in a position of trust must master their appetites, particularly those related to alcohol. It is a call to self-discipline and mental clarity, essential qualities for guiding other believers toward the truth.

sens: To listen, to disappear into the past
To be past, accomplished
G3944.detail:
1. The verb speaks of time that flows and disappears: the previous generations have "passed," meaning they belong to the bygone past. It is the image of a river that flows away. In Acts 14:16, Paul says that in the "past ages," meaning before the Gospel, God allowed the nations to walk in their own ways — that time is now behind us, gone.
2. The word emphasizes less the action than the final state: what has "passed" is completely accomplished and definitively gone. It is a closed, finished event that has no direct effect anymore.
G3944.origine: The verb is composed of παρά (beside, next to) and the verb οἴχομαι (to go away, to disappear). The basic image is therefore: "to go away beside us," "to surpass us by vanishing." This common word in Greek denotes the passage of time as something that escapes us and leaves us behind.
G3944.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 14:16, in the perfect participle form ("passed"). Paul uses it to refer to the ancient ages, before God's revelation through the Gospel. The context shows that God, during those past times, tolerated the nations following their own ways — a tolerance that has now ended with the coming of Christ and the call to repentance.
G3944.portee: This word reminds us that human history flows according to God's plan, and that each era has its times. The past ages are not lost or ignored by God: He governed them with intentional patience, in view of a final revelation. For the believer, this invites us to see that our time also fits into a divine purpose that is being fulfilled.

sens: To have the appearance of something
To be similar to, to share common traits with
G3945.detail:
1. To have the appearance of something: the word denotes an outward resemblance, the one that is seen at first glance. In Matthew 23:27, Jesus tells the Pharisees that they "resemble whitewashed tombs" — they look beautiful and well-kept on the outside, but the inside is filled with corruption and death.
2. To be similar to, to share common traits with: this is a broader resemblance, which can pertain to both substance and form. The verb emphasizes that the comparison is accurate and relevant: the Pharisees only appear to be holy, just as the whitewashed tombs only appear to be pure.
G3945.origine: The word comes from the prefix "para" (beside, similar to) and "homoios" (similar, of the same kind). It is a verb formed to express the idea of resembling, of making a comparison. The root "homoios" also appears in other Greek words in the New Testament that deal with resemblance: "homoiōsis" (resemblance), "homoios" (similar).
G3945.emploi: The verb appears only once in the preserved New Testament, in Matthew 23:27. Jesus uses it in a context of criticism against the hypocrisy of the scribes and Pharisees: he denounces their practice that highlights the outward appearance while hiding a rotten inner reality. This passage is at the heart of Matthew chapter 23, where Jesus pronounces a series of "woes" against those who claim piety without living it out.
G3945.portee: This word invites the Christian reader not to be deceived by appearances: a beautiful religious facade says nothing about the true state of the heart. For the disciple, it is a call to seek sincerity and inner transformation rather than external prestige, and to remain vigilant against false prophets and teachers who preach without practicing.

sens: Of the same nature or appearance
That resembles, that has the same quality as
Comparable, of the same order
G3946.detail:
1. The word describes what has a similar nature or appearance: two things that resemble each other. It is an adjective that expresses resemblance or equivalence. In Mark 7:13, Jesus speaks of the human traditions that the Pharisees "establish" and "do many other similar things" — other traditions of the same type, equally contrary to the Word of God.

2. The word can also emphasize a comparison or equivalence: things that belong to the same order, the same level. Human traditions are similar to one another in that they compete with the authority of the Word of God — they claim to have the same weight.

3. Figuratively, this extends to everything that has the same moral or spiritual quality: similar acts, similar principles. In Mark, it serves to show the uniformity of Pharisaic practice: one tradition begets another, all contrary to the Law.
G3946.origine: The word comes from the Greek prefix "para" (beside) and "homoios" (similar, alike). This composition suggests a resemblance of proximity: something that is "beside" the model, which is similar or comparable to it. The root "homoios" itself is ancient in Greek and always denotes a similarity or equivalence of nature. In the translation of the Greek Old Testament, words of the same family are found to translate the Hebrew "domé" (to resemble, to be alike).
G3946.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament (Mark 7:8 and 7:13), both in the same passage where Jesus criticizes the traditions of the Pharisees. In Mark 7:8, it concerns the "traditions of men"; in Mark 7:13, the "similar things" that the Pharisees do — other traditions of the same type. The context is polemical: Jesus shows how these human traditions, all similar to one another, nullify the Word of God. The word emphasizes the uniformity and systematic nature of the deviant practice.
G3946.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize how an initial disobedience begets others of the same type: a human tradition opens the door to a thousand others. For the Christian, it is a call to discern the difference between the Word of God and what is "similar" to it — what may seem harmless or pious but secretly opposes God's authority.

sens: Sharpen a weapon, make it sharp
Encourage someone to act, incite
Provoke anger, exasperate someone
G3947.detail:
1. In its literal and original sense, the word refers to the action of sharpening a blade or weapon to make it sharper — this is the primary image of the Greek verb. In classical Greek, this concrete meaning disappears, replaced by figurative meanings.
2. In a more active usage, the verb means to stimulate or push someone to do something, as one would urge a horse to move forward. It is a call to action, an impulse given from the outside.
3. The most common meaning in the Bible is to provoke anger or irritation: to disturb someone deeply to the point of making them angry. When Paul arrives in Athens and sees the city filled with idols, his spirit is irritated — he feels an inner irritation at this sight (Acts 17:16). In 1 Corinthians 13:5, love is not irritable: it is not easily exasperated or provoked to anger by the faults or shortcomings of others.
G3947.origine: The word is composed of the prefix παρ- ("beside," "in addition") and οξύνω ("make sharp," "sharpen"), derived from the adjective οξύς ("sharp," "pointed"). This root evokes the concrete image of a blade being sharpened by rubbing: one obtains a sharp point. In classical Greek, the verb has taken on figurative meanings: sharpening the mind becomes "stimulating," and sharpening someone's anger becomes "making them angry." The Bible uses it to translate Hebrew roots expressing anger or provocation.
G3947.emploi: The verb appears twice in the Segond translation, both times in the sense of "irritate." In Acts 17:16, Paul visits Athens and his spirit is irritated at the sight of the idols filling the city: this is an emotional reaction, almost involuntary, in response to what offends his faith. In 1 Corinthians 13:5, the Apostle Paul describes what love is not: love is not easily irritated, it is not provoked to anger by the actions or words of others. The context shows that the word denotes an inner agitation, a rise of anger or exasperation, rather than an external action.
G3947.portee: This word highlights two important realities for the believer. First, it acknowledges that the emotional reaction to idolatry or evil is natural and just: Paul is irritated because his love for God is sincere. But then, 1 Corinthians 13 teaches us that spiritual maturity consists in not being dominated by this irritability: true love remains calm and patient, it is not easily provoked. It is a call to cultivate a proper reaction without falling into destructive anger.

sens: Stimulation, incitement to act or react
Acute irritation, tension that leads to separation
G3948.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a stimulation or provocation in a positive sense: something that pushes someone to act, to mobilize. In Hebrews 10:24, "stir up to love" means "to encourage one another to practice love and good works" — it is a benevolent provocation, a spur that awakens the commitment of believers.
2. The same word can also describe an acute irritation or annoyance that creates tension. In Acts 15:39, the "contention was sharp" between Paul and Barnabas: this mutual provocation, this irritation between them, was strong enough to separate them. The image is that of a spark igniting the spirits.
G3948.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "to provoke" or "to irritate" (itself formed from "beside" and "to sharpen"). Its basic image is that of a spike, a point that annoys or stimulates. This family of words in Greek often translates in the Greek Old Testament the Hebrew "fury" or "anger," but the primary meaning remains that of a provocation, a stimulation — which can be good or bad depending on the context.
G3948.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Acts 15:39, it describes the irritation that opposes Paul and Barnabas in Jerusalem: the "sharp contention" over the issue of Mark creates a tension that leads to their separation and two distinct missionary journeys. In Hebrews 10:24, the same word is used in a positive sense: "let us stir one another up to love" is a call to mutually stimulate one another for the practice of love. The context thus determines whether the provocation is beneficial or harmful.
G3948.portee: This word invites the believer to discern two uses of provocation: that which divides and that which builds up. The Bible does not condemn all tension or confrontation, but it exhorts Christians to "provoke" one another toward good, as in Hebrews. The account in Acts also shows that even good servants (Paul and Barnabas) can be swept away by irritation; it is a call to vigilance over our reactions and humility in our disagreements.

sens: Stir up anger in someone
Irritate someone through words or actions
Push to jealousy or envy
G3949.detail: 1. It means to make someone angry, to make them furious: one acts in a way that ignites their anger. In Romans 10:19, Moses announces that God "will provoke to jealousy" Israel by a nation that is not a people — it is about creating in them an intense feeling of envy or irritation at the salvation granted to others. 2. It also means to irritate someone daily through an attitude or words that annoy them. In Ephesians 6:4, Paul tells fathers not to "provoke" their children — not to exasperate, hurt, or exacerbate them with unreasonable commands, but rather to raise them with discipline and instruction. 3. The word emphasizes the idea of a reaction that is provoked: it is not a simple light annoyance, but an intentional or effective triggering of emotion.
G3949.origine: The word comes from the prefix para ("beside," "against") added to orguê, which means "anger" or "irritation." The image is that of something pushing against anger, setting it in motion. It is a Greek verb that often translates in the Old Testament Hebrew the word käas ("provoke to anger," "irritate"), used notably in scenes where God or a person pushes another to fury.
G3949.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Romans 10:19, Paul cites Moses to explain that God will provoke the Jews to jealousy by granting salvation to the nations — it is a voluntary and pedagogical provocation, intended to awaken Israel. In Ephesians 6:4, it is a warning addressed to fathers: do not irritate your children with an authoritarian or unjust attitude. Both usages emphasize an action that affects the emotions of others, either for a divine purpose or in a daily relationship.
G3949.portee: This word invites the Christian father to be vigilant: education must correct and instruct, certainly, but without instilling frustration or hurt in the child. It also reminds us that God sometimes provokes our jealousy or reaction to bring us back to Him. It is a lesson on the weight of our words and actions on those around us.

sens: A feeling of intense annoyance, more sudden and less deep than a lasting anger
A state of agitation of the soul provoked by an offense or annoyance
Temporary outburst, fit of indignation
G3950.detail:
1. It is an anger that rises quickly, a sharp irritation of the soul in response to what displeases or offends us, but it remains more superficial and less enduring than a truly rooted anger. It is like a flame that suddenly rises rather than a fire that smolders for a long time.

2. This word describes the emotional state of one who feels provoked or insulted — it is not cold and calculated rage, but rather that turmoil of the soul that arises in the face of injustice or affront (Ephesians 4:26 warns: even this irritated anger can lead us to sin if we allow it to dominate).

3. It is a movement of indignation, a flare-up of emotion rather than a lasting disposition. Paul distinguishes this kind of anger, which one may experience for a moment, from a rooted and persistent hostility that would corrupt an entire day.
G3950.origine: The word comes from the prefix "par" (beside, near) and "orge" (anger, wrath). This formation suggests an anger that arises, that adds on, that comes "beside" rather than an anger that settles in for the long term. The underlying Hebrew root in the Old Testament translated by this Greek word speaks to the same idea of temporary irritation in response to an offense.
G3950.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament: in Ephesians 4:26, where Paul quotes Psalm 4:5 and allows believers to experience anger without falling into sin. The context shows that it is a legitimate anger but dangerous if it persists beyond a day. It is an anger that can seize us in the face of injustice, but which we must refuse to let settle and ferment.
G3950.portee: This word teaches us that there is an anger that is not intrinsically sinful — Paul does not tell us to never be angry, but not to let this irritated anger lead us to act wrongly or consume us from within. It is an invitation to recognize our emotions while mastering them quickly, before the end of the day, so as not to give the devil a foothold.

sens: To urge someone to act, to push them to do something
To provoke an action or reaction in a crowd or community
G3951.detail:
1. To incite means to push someone to act, to strongly encourage them to do something. It is an impulse communicated to a person to set them in motion or action. In Acts 13:50, the Jews incite the devout women, meaning they push them to turn against Paul and Barnabas.
2. The word also describes the action of provoking a collective action or reaction from a community. The Jews incite the city leaders, which leads to persecution: they create a movement of opposition and hostility from almost nothing, through persuasion or influence.
G3951.origine: The Greek word comes from a preposition (παρά, "beside") and a verb meaning "to prick, to sting." The image is that of prodding an animal to make it move, hence the sense of stimulating or pushing someone to action. This verb was used by ancient Greek writers (found in Hippocrates and others) to describe the action of inciting.
G3951.emploi: The word appears only once in Acts 13:50. Paul and Barnabas are preaching in Antioch of Pisidia; the Jews, jealous of their success, do not content themselves with opposing directly, but incite the devout women and the authorities of the city against the two apostles. This incitement leads to organized persecution that results in the expulsion of the missionaries. The context shows that the incitement is a malicious action: it is to stir up hostility in others to reach one's enemies.
G3951.portee: This verse reminds us that hatred and opposition to the message of the Gospel can come through insidious means: instead of confronting directly, one seeks to incite others against the preachers. For the Christian, it is a warning: to know that those who oppose the faith may act this way, and to remain steadfast despite the persecutions stirred up by the malicious influence of others.

sens: The fact of being present, physical presence
The arrival, the coming of someone
The solemn coming of Christ at the end of times, his glorious return
G3952.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the simple fact of being present somewhere. Paul writes to the Corinthians that the presence of the body is weak, in contrast to absence: it is the ordinary physical presence of a person (2 Corinthians 10:10).
2. It is then an arrival, a coming that is awaited. When Paul writes that he rejoices at the coming of Stephanas, he is simply talking about his arrival (1 Corinthians 16:17). It is a concrete event: someone we are waiting for finally arrives.
3. In the New Testament, the word takes on exceptional significance: it denotes the Coming of Christ, his glorious and solemn arrival at the end of times. Jesus asks his disciples: "What will be the sign of your coming?" (Matthew 24:3). It is the moment when Christ will resurrect the dead and judge the world (1 Corinthians 15:23), the most important event that Christians await.
G3952.origine: The Greek word combines two elements: "par" (beside) and "to be present." It literally denotes the action of being beside someone, of being present. In Greco-Roman antiquity, it became a technical term for the official visit of a king or dignitary. The New Testament applies this majestic word to the return of Christ, as if he were coming to visit his people in glory.
G3952.emploi: The word appears 24 times in the New Testament, especially in Paul's epistles and in the later epistles. It is used 3 times for ordinary arrivals (Stephanas, Timothy, Titus: 1 Corinthians 16:17; 2 Corinthians 7:6-7; Philippians 1:26), and 2 times for simple physical presence (2 Corinthians 10:10; Philippians 2:12). But in 17 instances, it denotes the eschatological Coming of Christ: it is the key term in passages where Jesus or Paul speaks of the final judgment, the resurrection of the dead, and the renewal of all things. Paul frequently returns to this in his letters to the Thessalonians, who were anxiously questioning him about the timing of this event.
G3952.portee: This word carries at the heart of Christian hope. It reminds the reader that Christ is not just an event of the past, but a living reality who will return. The Coming is not an abstract doctrine: it is the promise that the Lord will restore all things, judge evil, and dwell with his people. This expectation transforms the present life of the believer, who strives to remain vigilant and pure while awaiting this coming.

sens: tableware intended for serving dishes and sauces
dish served, tasty accompaniment
that which appears beautiful outwardly but is defiled inwardly
G3953.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a plate, that is, a piece of tableware, often shallow, on which food is presented to guests. This is the literal meaning of the word.
2. By extension, it can also refer to the content itself — the delicate dishes or sauces — rather than the container that holds them, as one might say 'a good dish' to refer to the food rather than the porcelain plate.
3. In Jesus' teaching, the word takes on a figurative meaning: in Matthew 23:25-26, Jesus speaks of the 'plate' in parallel with the 'cup', to criticize the Pharisees who are concerned with cleaning the outside of the plate — its appearance — but leave the inside defiled by greed and intemperance. The plate thus becomes a symbol of a life whose appearance is purified, but not its reality.
G3953.origine: The Greek word comes from the preposition 'beside' (para) and a root meaning 'to eat' or 'that which is eaten' (opson). It literally means 'what is eaten beside', 'the accompaniment'. In classical Greek, the word was considered less noble by language purists (the Atticists), who preferred other terms. It belongs to the simple, concrete vocabulary of daily life.
G3953.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 23, verses 25 and 26. Jesus uses it in his discourse against the hypocritical scribes and Pharisees. He associates the 'plate' with the 'cup', both representing the container and the content. Here, the context is not gastronomic: the plate becomes an image to express the contrast between outward appearance and inner reality. Jesus denounces a religion that stops at external splendor while the inside remains tainted by injustice and disorder.
G3953.portee: This passage invites the Christian to examine their own life: not to settle for a superficial piety, but to seek the purity of heart. The 'plate' reminds us that God sees beyond appearances and that true transformation begins from within. It is a call to authenticity in faith, where actions and intentions must correspond to the outward profession of faith.

sens: Freedom of speech, the way of expressing oneself without hesitation or fear
Boldness, confidence without fear in the presence of someone superior
The act of speaking or acting openly, without hiding
Calm confidence before God in prayer
G3954.detail:
1. Assurance is primarily the freedom to speak frankly and without restraint. It is to express oneself by saying everything one thinks, without sparing the truth: when Jesus speaks 'openly' in John 11:14, he hides nothing from his disciples. The apostles preach 'freely' in Acts 2:29 because they are no longer afraid to speak the truth.
2. It also denotes boldness, the absence of fear in the presence of someone greater or more powerful. Paul says he 'has assurance' in Philippians 1:20 despite his trial. It is an inner confidence that drives away fear.
3. It can mean to act or show oneself 'publicly', without hiding. Colossians 2:15 says that Jesus 'disarmed the powers and authorities, and made a public spectacle of them': he defeated them openly, without secret.
4. It is the peaceful confidence with which one approaches God to pray. Hebrews 10:19 speaks of a 'bold entrance into the sanctuary' through the blood of Jesus: the believer can enter before God without hesitation or fear of judgment.
G3954.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and literally means 'to say everything' (from 'all' and 'word'). It originally designates the freedom of speech that characterized Athenian democracy, where every citizen could express themselves without fear. In the Greek Bible, it also translates the Hebrew idea of boldness and confidence. Over time, the word has enriched: from simple 'freedom of speech' it has evolved to 'courageous confidence' and 'trust in God'.
G3954.emploi: The word appears 31 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul's epistles and in the Gospel of John. In the Gospels (Mark, John), it primarily means to speak openly, without hesitation: Jesus speaks 'openly' or asks questions without reserve. In Acts, it denotes the boldness of the apostles who preach despite threats: they speak 'freely' about Jesus. In the epistles, particularly Hebrews and 1 John, it nuances: it is the peaceful confidence of the believer who approaches God in prayer, knowing they are accepted by grace. Paul also uses it to express courageous confidence in the face of trials.
G3954.portee: This word reminds the believer that they can speak frankly with God in prayer, without fear or mask. Thanks to Jesus, access to the Father is no longer closed by fear of judgment. Assurance is also a fruit of the Holy Spirit in the life of the witness: it enables disciples to testify publicly despite dangers. It is a call to joyful freedom and confidence that characterize life in Christ.

sens: Express one's thoughts without restraint or fear
Preach the Gospel with assurance and frankness
Testify publicly, despite opposition or danger
G3955.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is to speak without restraint: to say everything one thinks, openly and without reservation. In Acts 18:26, Apollos 'spoke freely in the synagogue', without hesitation before his audience. It is a word that hides nothing, that does not fear exposure.
2. The word takes on a specifically religious hue: to speak freely about faith, to preach the Gospel with assurance. In Acts 14:3, the apostles 'spoke boldly', relying on the Lord, and announced the grace of God without reservation or compromise. It is a boldness that comes from conviction.
3. More broadly, it means to testify publicly despite hostility. In Acts 13:46, Paul declares to the unbelieving Jews 'with assurance' that the Gospel will turn to the Gentiles: it is a courageous frankness that confronts rejection. In Acts 19:8, Paul 'spoke freely' for three months in the synagogue in a way that persuaded — a bold persistence.
G3955.origine: The word comes from παρρησία (parrhésia), composed of πᾶν (pan, 'all') and ῥῆσις (rhésis, 'speech'), hence literally 'to say all'. It primarily designates freedom of speech, then boldness and frankness. The root evokes the idea of holding nothing back, of expressing oneself without censorship. In the Greek Old Testament, the verb notably translates the Hebrew שׂנח (nōaḥ) in a sense of joyful boldness (Job 22:26), which reinforces the image of a word that flourishes freely.
G3955.emploi: The verb appears 8 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in Acts (6 occurrences) and a bit in the epistles. It typically characterizes apostolic preaching after Pentecost. Paul and the other apostles 'speak freely' the Gospel: in the face of the Jews (Acts 13:46), in the synagogues (Acts 18:26, 19:8), before authorities (Acts 9:27, 26:26). In Acts 14:3, this frankness is presented as a sign of the Lord's support who confirms his word through miracles. In Ephesians 6:20 and 1 Thessalonians 2:2, Paul asks for prayers or recalls having spoken with this same boldness grounded in faith. The word illustrates one of the major transformations of the disciple: fear becomes boldness through the presence of the Holy Spirit.
G3955.portee: This word invites the Christian to recognize that the testimony of faith is not a matter of timidity or compromise. The apostles were able to preach 'freely' despite threats and hostility because their confidence rested on God, not on human approval. For the contemporary reader, it is a call to a certain spiritual boldness: not to be afraid to express one's conviction, not out of impulsiveness, but out of fidelity to the received truth and because one is supported by the Lord.

sens: each thing, each person, without exception
the totality of something as a whole
every kind, every sort, of any nature
G3956.detail:
1. The word "all" refers to each element of a group without leaving any out. It can qualify people ("all men"), objects ("all the loaves"), or situations ("in every circumstance"). For example, in Matthew 4:23, Jesus goes through "all Galilee," meaning every region, every city of that province.
2. "All" also expresses the complete whole, the totality considered as a unified block. This is the sense of "everything that exists" or "the entire universe." In John 1:3, "all things were made by the Word," which means: the entire universe depends on Christ.
3. Finally, "all" can mean "of all kinds" or "without restriction." In Matthew 4:4, Jesus says that man does not live by bread alone, but by "every word," meaning each word, of whatever kind it may be.
G3956.origine: This word comes from an ancient Greek root that expresses the absence of limit and completeness. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it usually translates the word "kol," which also means "totality" and "each unit." The Greek word declines according to gender and number to fit the noun it qualifies.
G3956.emploi: "All" is one of the most frequent words in the New Testament: over 1,000 occurrences. It appears in all the books, particularly in the Gospels and the letters of Paul. Sometimes it qualifies a noun without an article ("every man"), sometimes with the article ("all men"), which slightly affects the nuance. Alone or with a noun, it reinforces the idea of universality: "at all times," "all hope," "all power." When it is a pronoun ("all"), it designates the entirety of the people referred to. In Acts 27:20, "all hope" of being saved had disappeared, which expresses total dispossession.
G3956.portee: This word reminds the reader that God sees, knows, and governs the entirety of creation and history, without exception. Understanding the biblical meaning of "all" helps to grasp the universality of grace, human responsibility, and the reign of Christ: there is nothing outside of His authority.

sens: The Jewish feast commemorating the liberation from Egypt and the protection of the firstborn of Israel
The festive meal taken during this celebration
The lamb sacrificed and eaten during this meal
(Figuratively) Christ, considered as the lamb sacrificed for salvation
G3957.detail:
1. The Passover is the major annual feast of the Jewish calendar, celebrated in the spring to commemorate the foundational event recounted in Exodus 12: the tenth plague of Egypt, when God struck down the Egyptian firstborn but spared the houses of the Israelites whose doorposts were marked with the blood of a lamb. It is the moment when God liberated Israel from slavery (Matthew 26:2, Luke 22:1).
2. By extension, the word also refers to the solemn meal eaten during this feast, where the family gathers to consume the roasted lamb with bitter herbs and unleavened bread (Matthew 26:18, 26:19).
3. The term also designates the lamb itself, the animal sacrificed according to the prescribed rite (Mark 14:12, Luke 22:7).
4. The Apostle Paul sees in Jesus Christ the fulfillment of the deep meaning of Passover: He is "our Passover" sacrificed for us (1 Corinthians 5:7), the lamb whose sacrifice redeems and protects believers from divine judgment.
G3957.origine: The word pascha comes from Aramaic טַּסְחָא (tascha), which itself comes from Hebrew פֶּסַח (pessakh). This Hebrew name literally means "to pass over" or "to spare," from the verb פָּסַח (pasakh): it is because the Angel of the Lord "passed over" the houses marked with the blood of the lamb that they were spared. The word thus directly refers to God's saving act at the time of the liberation from Egypt.
G3957.emploi: Passover is mentioned 27 times in the New Testament, especially in the Gospels and Acts. Each Gospel reports the preparations for Passover before the crucifixion of Jesus: where to prepare the meal, how to partake of it (Matthew 26:17-19, Mark 14:12-16, Luke 22:7-13). John mentions Passover several times to situate the events of Jesus' life (John 2:13, 6:4, 11:55, 12:1, 13:1), as a major chronological marker. The word designates either the festival as a whole (John 18:39), the specific meal (Matthew 26:18-19), or the lamb (Mark 14:12). In 1 Corinthians 5:7, Paul makes an interpretive shift by making Jesus the true Passover, which transforms the Christian understanding of this word: Jesus replaces and fulfills the figure of the Passover lamb.
G3957.portee: For the believer, understanding the meaning of the word Passover helps to comprehend why the crucifixion of Jesus occurs precisely at this feast, and how the life, death, and resurrection of Christ truly fulfill what Passover foreshadowed: a passage from death to life, a radical liberation, a protection granted by God to those who turn to His sacrifice. This is why Christian churches remind each year, at Easter, that Christ is the true lamb who saves us and frees us from sin.

sens: To experience physical or emotional pain
To undergo harm, injury, or injustice
To endure, to bear what is painful
To suffer from an illness or infirmity
To experience difficult things (in a broad sense)
To feel a painful emotion
G3958.detail:
1. To experience physical or emotional pain: the word describes the state of one who feels harm within themselves, whether physical or from the heart. For example: Jesus says that he must "suffer" many things at the hands of the elders and chief priests (Matthew 16:21) — this means to undergo mistreatment and affliction.

2. To undergo harm, injury, or injustice: to suffer means to be a victim, to receive wrong. A believer who "suffers" because they do what is right endures unjustly (1 Peter 2:20) — they do not deserve it, but they endure it for their conscience toward God.

3. To endure, to bear what is painful: suffering includes the idea of perseverance in the face of trial. The disciples who "suffer" with Christ learn to hold on despite the pain (Hebrews 5:8 shows the Son learning obedience through what he suffered).

4. To suffer from an illness or infirmity: this means to experience the effects of physical harm. The woman who had been suffering from a flow of blood for twelve years and had suffered much at the hands of physicians (Mark 5:26) embodies this concrete reality.

5. To experience difficult things in a broad sense: suffering can extend to any form of going through trials. Paul says, "I suffer these things" (2 Timothy 1:12) when speaking of the chains and persecutions he endures for the Gospel.

6. To feel a painful emotion in solidarity: when one member of the body suffers, all the members "suffer" with them (1 Corinthians 12:26) — this is sharing in another's pain out of compassion.
G3958.origine: The verb comes from a Greek root that primarily means "to undergo an action," "to be affected by something from the outside." It contrasts with the verb "to act": one who suffers receives harm rather than inflicting it. In biblical Hebrew, it sometimes renders the verb חָלָה ("to be sick, to become weak"), which shows that suffering weakens and diminishes. The word generally has a negative connotation — suffering is not sought, it comes — except when it is endured voluntarily for a good cause.
G3958.emploi: The verb appears 41 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and the Apostle Peter. It primarily refers to the suffering of Christ: all four Gospels report it, and it is a constant theme (Luke 24:46: "the Christ would suffer, and rise from the dead"). Paul uses it to speak of his own persecution (2 Timothy 1:12, Acts 9:16). Peter uses it abundantly to exhort believers to patiently endure hostility (1 Peter 2:19-23, 3:17-18, 4:1, 4:15, 4:19). The verb can stand alone ("to suffer" without a complement) or with specifications: to suffer "at the hands of" someone (Matthew 16:21), to suffer "for" the Gospel (Acts 9:16), to suffer "much" or "a little" (Revelation 2:10). In 1 Corinthians 12:26, the context is that of the Church as a body, and the verb expresses solidarity: the suffering of one member affects the whole.
G3958.portee: This word calls the Christian to consider suffering not as an absurdity, but as an inseparable reality of life in this world — and especially of life with Christ. Jesus himself suffered: this gives meaning and dignity to the suffering of the believer. The verb also invites compassion toward those who suffer and solidarity within the body of Christ. Finally, it reminds us that suffering endured for obeying God is not a shame, but a grace (1 Peter 2:20).

sens: Maritime port of Lycia, region of Roman Asia Minor
G3959.detail: Patara is an important port city on the southwestern coast of Asia Minor, in the ancient region of Lycia (modern-day Turkey). In Acts 21:1, Paul and his companions arrive at Patara during their return journey to Jerusalem after leaving Tyre. It is there that they take a ship to cross the Mediterranean. Patara was known as a major commercial center and a strategic natural harbor on the maritime route to Syria and Judea.
G3959.origine: The name Patara designates this port city of the Greco-Roman world. Its exact etymological meaning is less clear, but the name is well attested in ancient geography as that of a prosperous city in Lycia.
G3959.emploi: Patara appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 21:1. It is mentioned in the account of Paul's third missionary journey, at the moment he is returning from his ministry in Asia Minor and Greece to go to Jerusalem. The mention of Patara situates the itinerary of the journey: after Cos and Rhodes, it is the port of embarkation for the final destination.

sens: To deliver a violent blow to someone with a weapon or the hand
To reach or mortally wound
To affect or reach (in a figurative sense, like a disease or plague)
G3960.detail:
1. To strike means to deliver a violent blow to someone, usually with a weapon. When the disciple draws his sword at Gethsemane, he "strikes" the servant of the high priest and cuts off his ear (Luke 22:50). This is a brutal, immediate, physical act.

2. The word also designates a mortal blow or a serious injury. Jesus cites the prophecy: "I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered" (Matthew 26:31) — here, "to strike" means to reach mortally, with a destructive impact.

3. In a figurative sense, to strike describes how a disease or plague reaches someone. The angel strikes Herod (Acts 12:23), and in Revelation, God's witnesses strike the earth with plagues (Revelation 11:6) — the word then expresses a divine action that affects, judges, and spiritually wounds.
G3960.origine: The Greek verb πατάσσω (patassō) is related to πλήσσω (plēssō), which also means "to strike" or "to hit." It regularly translates the Hebrew verb נָכָה (naka, "to strike") in the intensive form in the Greek Old Testament. This root evokes the image of a blow delivered with force, whether physically or in a figurative sense (a calamity that "strikes").
G3960.emploi: The verb appears 10 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. It is used first in a literal sense: when Peter strikes the servant of the high priest (Matthew 26:51, Luke 22:50), or when Moses strikes an Egyptian to defend a Hebrew (Acts 7:24). Luke reports the disciples' question: "Shall we strike with the sword?" (Luke 22:49). The word is also used in quotations from the Old Testament, notably Zechariah 13:7: "I will strike the shepherd" (Matthew 26:31, Mark 14:27), announcing divine judgment. Finally, it takes on a figurative sense when it designates the action of disease or judgment: the angel strikes Herod (Acts 12:23), and in Revelation, the witnesses strike the earth with plagues (Revelation 11:6, 19:15).
G3960.portee: This word helps the reader grasp the reality of violence in biblical narratives — not as an abstraction, but as a concrete act. It also shows how God acts: not through gentleness, but sometimes through judgment that "strikes." Understanding that Jesus announces he will be struck (like the shepherd) helps to measure the weight of the Passion: it is not a simple death, but the blow of God that falls upon him for our salvation.

sens: To walk on something, to place the foot on
To trample, crush underfoot
To dominate, master by force
To profane, defile by occupation or invasion
G3961.detail:
1. The simplest meaning: to walk on something, to place the foot on it. Jesus tells his disciples: "I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions" (Luke 10:19) — this is not malice, but the assurance of being able to traverse dangers without fear.
2. To crush, trample with force, as when one treads grapes in the winepress (Revelation 14:20: "the winepress was trodden outside the city"). It is a destructive, violent crushing.
3. To dominate, conquer by force: Jerusalem will be "trodden down by the nations" (Luke 21:24), meaning that its enemies will dominate and occupy it. It is an image of defeat and submission.
4. To profane, defile a holy place: "the nations will tread down the holy city" (Revelation 11:2) refers to enemy occupation and the desecration of the temple. It is also an act of contempt for what is sacred.
G3961.origine: The Greek verb πατέω comes from a root that evokes the action of placing the foot, of walking. It particularly translates the Hebrew דָּרַךְ (dārak), which literally means "to tread, to walk on." In the Old Testament, this Hebrew verb is used in a concrete sense (to walk on a path) and in a figurative sense (to dominate, to conquer). The Greek retains these two dimensions: the physical act of treading and the idea of domination or profanation.
G3961.emploi: The verb παπατέω appears 5 times in the Segond translations. It is first used in the physical sense: to tread on (Luke 10:19, where Jesus speaks of treading on serpents). But its dominant usage is figurative: to tread means "to trample, to crush," especially in the apocalyptic context where grapes are trodden in the winepress (Revelation 14:20, 19:15). The meaning is also that of dominating by conquest: "Jerusalem will be trodden down by the nations" (Luke 21:24, Revelation 11:2) expresses enemy occupation and humiliation. This last usage is close to biblical Hebrew, where to tread a people means to dominate and oppress them.
G3961.portee: For the Christian reader, this word teaches spiritual victory (Luke 10:19: authority over the powers of evil) and also humility in the face of divine judgment (treading the grapes in the winepress of judgment). It also reminds that Jerusalem will experience a period of oppression before its restoration. The verb reveals how the Bible speaks of power: sometimes that which God grants to the believer, sometimes that which hostile forces exercise.

sens: The man who has begotten a child, his male parent
The distant ancestor of a person or people
One who has created, founded, or originated something
A person in a position of authority, wisdom, or responsibility
God as creator and protector
God as the father of Jesus Christ
G3962.detail:
1. The father is the male parent, the one who has begotten the child: Herod is the father of Jesus according to civil law (Matthew 2:22), Zebedee is the father of James and John (Matthew 4:21). The word also designates both parents together (Hebrews 11:23: "by faith, his parents hid him").
2. The fathers are the ancestors, those from whom one descends: God is called "the God of our fathers" (Acts 5:30), Abraham is the father of believers (Romans 4:11). This meaning refers to the entire chain of past generations.
3. The father is one who creates or causes something: the devil is presented as the father of lies (John 8:44), for he is its origin and author. Likewise, God is the father of lights, their source and creator (James 1:17).
4. Masters, elders, those who teach and govern with responsibility are called "fathers": Jesus says that no one should be called "father" on earth for spiritual matters (Matthew 23:9), for only God deserves this title of absolute authority.
5. God is the father of all created things, of all living beings: he is "above all, and through all, and in all" (Ephesians 4:6). This divine fatherhood encompasses the entire universe.
6. Jesus calls God his Father in a unique relationship: Jesus says "my Father" and teaches us to pray "our Father" (Matthew 6:9), thus opening to believers a filial relationship with God that the Old Testament prepared.
G3962.origine: The Greek word "patēr" comes from a very ancient root common to many Indo-European languages, that of Latin "pater" and French "père". In Hebrew, the main word is "ab" (אָב), which the Greek translation of the Old Testament almost always renders as "patēr". The root evokes the image of power, generation, and responsibility: the father is one who begets and nourishes.
G3962.emploi: The word "father" appears more than 370 times in the New Testament, particularly in Matthew and John. It first simply designates the biological father (Matthew 2:22, Luke 1:59), then expands to the meaning of ancestor (Acts 5:30: "the God of our fathers"). The New Testament adds a prophetic dimension: Jesus constantly speaks of his heavenly Father, especially in the Gospel of John, establishing a filial intimacy (John 11:41). The apostle Paul develops the idea that Christians are children of God, heirs with Christ, through the Spirit of adoption (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). The word can also designate the author or origin of something (John 8:44: the devil, father of lies) or a figure of spiritual authority (Matthew 23:9: Jesus' warning against masters who call themselves "fathers").
G3962.portee: Understanding this word transforms the prayer and trust of the Christian. Jesus does not just teach us that God exists, but that he is our Father — someone benevolent, who knows our needs, who protects and forgives us. This filial relationship, at the heart of the Gospel, changes everything: it frees from the fear of judgment and opens to the joy of being unconditionally loved. It is also a moral responsibility: if God is our Father, we are brothers to one another.

sens: Island in the Aegean Sea where the apostle John received the Revelation
G3963.detail: Patmos is a small island in the Aegean Sea, off the coast of Asia Minor. It is where the apostle John was exiled and where he received the visions of Revelation, as he himself affirms at the beginning of his book: "I was on the island called Patmos, because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus" (Revelation 1:9). This island thus becomes the place from which the last book of the New Testament emerges.
G3963.origine: Patmos is a real island in the Dodecanese archipelago in the eastern Mediterranean. Its name is of ancient Greek origin. Ancient Christian tradition places John's exile there, probably during the persecutions under Emperor Domitian at the end of the 1st century.
G3963.emploi: The island of Patmos appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 1:9. It is the setting for John's prophetic ministry. According to this verse, John was sent or exiled to this island "because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus," meaning due to his faithfulness to the Christian message. It is in this isolated place that he received the revelations he records in his book.

sens: one who strikes his father
one who kills his father
in a broader sense: one who commits a crime against his father
G3964.detail: 1. The word literally means one who strikes or wounds his father — a stark image of the crime. 2. It more specifically refers to one who kills his father, one of the worst crimes a society can know. In 1 Timothy 1:9, Paul lists the most serious crimes that the law punishes: parricide is among them, alongside murderers, as an extreme violation of the respect due to parents.
G3964.origine: The word comes from two Greek roots: "patêr" meaning father, and "aloao" meaning to strike or wound. It is constructed on the same model as "mêtroloïas" (one who strikes his mother). It is an ancient term in classical Greek, forged to name an act considered a social and moral sacrilege.
G3964.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 1:9. Paul lists the different categories of sinners for whom the Law was given — not for the righteous, but to restrain serious crimes. He names parricides alongside murderers, rebels, and the ungodly. The context shows that Paul takes the reality of moral and legal evil seriously: some acts violate so deeply the order that God has established that they require legal correction. This is the only use of the term in Scripture.
G3964.portee: This verse reminds us that God's Law protects even the most sacred bonds — that between parent and child. It is not an arbitrary instrument, but a guard against crimes that destroy communal life. For the Christian, this also emphasizes that respect for our parents is not a detail: it is a commandment inscribed at the heart of the moral order that God wants to see prevail. This is how the grace of the Gospel transforms our hearts: not by abolishing the Law, but by giving us the ability to honor it.

sens: Group of people united by a common ancestry, a lineage
Clan or tribe, a set of families linked by blood
The entirety of all beings, celestial and terrestrial, that form the great family of God
G3965.detail:
1. The first occurrence shows familia in the strict genealogical sense: Joseph belongs to the "family of David," meaning he descends from David through a regular lineage. It is a chain of ancestors that gives a person their identity and rights (Luke 2:4).
2. In Acts 3:25, the word expands: "all the families of the earth will be blessed" refers to entire peoples, the large divisions of humanity. Here, family means rather clan or tribe, a human group organized around a common root.
3. In Ephesians 3:15, Paul uses the word in a nearly poetic way: "every family in heaven and on earth" derives its name from the Father. Here, the meaning becomes universal and spiritual — it is the great family of creatures, in heaven and on earth, that recognizes God as Father.
G3965.origine: The Greek word comes from "father" (patêr). A patria is literally what belongs to the father, the descent of the father, his extended household. In Hebrew, the word corresponds mainly to "mispacha" (family in the sense of clan), broader than the household (oikos) but narrower than the tribe (phylê). It is a term that emphasizes genealogical unity and the heritage passed from father to son.
G3965.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always in a genealogical or universal context. In Luke, it refers to Joseph's royal lineage. In Paul (Acts and Ephesians), it takes on a broader scope: first the entirety of earthly peoples as heirs of the promise to Abraham, then the totality of created beings that depend on God the Father. The word thus moves from the particular (a lineage) to the collective (a people) and then to the universal (every creature).
G3965.portee: This word reminds the Christian that their identity comes from their heritage, and ultimately from God the Father. For Luke, it emphasizes that Jesus is part of the concrete history of Israel. For Paul, it opens a grand vision: every created being, from the humblest to the highest, belongs to the family of God and can say "Our Father." It is a word of comfort and unity.

sens: the founding father of a tribe or people
the revered ancestor from whom several generations descend
one who exercises sovereign authority over his family and descendants
G3966.detail:
1. A patriarch is primarily the founding father of a large family, a tribe, or an entire people. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are called patriarchs (Acts 7:8) because they founded the twelve tribes of Israel: Jacob fathered the twelve patriarchs who became the nation.
2. The word also designates the distant ancestor from whom an entire community claims descent and to whom it refers. David is honored as a patriarch (Acts 2:29) because he is the father of the royal dynasty and all Israel recognizes itself in his lineage.
3. Finally, it is one who, by virtue of his age, wisdom, and status as an ancestor, exercises natural and respected authority over all his descendants and his household. Abraham was so great that even a king honored him: Melchizedek received tithes from Abraham the patriarch (Hebrews 7:4).
G3966.origine: The Greek word patriarchēs combines two roots: patria (the family, the clan) and archē (the command, the authority). It literally means the chief, the one who "commands" his patria. In Hebrew and Aramaic, it corresponds to ab (father) and expressions designating the head of the family or the prince of the clan. It is a word that expresses the natural power of the ancient father over all his descendants.
G3966.emploi: The New Testament uses this word 4 times, always in Acts and Hebrews, to speak of the founders of Israel. Acts 7:8 places it as a title of honor for the twelve sons of Jacob. Acts 7:9 shows that it is a word of authority: the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him, highlighting the power and respect attached to this title. Acts 2:29 applies the title to David, the king and father of the dynasty. Hebrews 7:4 emphasizes the greatness of the patriarch Abraham by recalling that even Melchizedek, priest of the Most High, received tithes from him.
G3966.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that the faith of Israel rests on founding figures of great moral and spiritual authority. The patriarchs are not just genealogical ancestors: they are the men who knew God, obeyed Him, and whose descendants were built on their Covenant. Understanding the role of the patriarch helps to grasp how the Bible conceives of spiritual heritage: not as a mere genetic transmission, but as a filiation in faith and in covenant with God.

sens: belonging to the father or coming from the father
concerning ancestors and family tradition
what is passed down as inheritance from one generation to another
G3967.detail:
1. The word designates what belongs to the father or emanates from him: what is characteristic of fatherhood. In Galatians 1:14, Paul speaks of the "traditions of my fathers" — these customs and teachings that each generation received from the previous generation, tracing back to the ancestors of Israel.

2. This includes everything that relates to ancestors in a broad sense: not just the immediate father, but the heritage that a family or people holds from its origins. Paul says he was zealous for that heritage.

3. Therefore, it is what is transmitted, what comes from the past and is inscribed in the continuity of a lineage. The word emphasizes the hereditary, received, established nature.
G3967.origine: The word comes from the Greek pater (father) and belongs to the family of words that speak of fatherhood. It implies a transmission: what is paternal is what one receives from one's father or fathers. In Hebrew, this sentiment is expressed by the word concerning fathers (avot): paternal traditions are those that have been preserved and respected through generations.
G3967.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Galatians 1:14, where Paul testifies to his past zeal for traditions. At that time in his life before his conversion, he was fully devoted to preserving and practicing the religious heritage passed down to him by his ancestors, the ancestral traditions of Judaism. The context shows that he viewed this attachment as a source of pride, a form of religious perfection, before understanding that only faith in Christ mattered.
G3967.portee: This word invites the Christian to reflect on the difference between a human heritage, however noble, and the grace of Christ. Paul uses it to say that he had to renounce that zeal, however sincere it was, to receive new life in Jesus. It is a lesson on the insufficiency of religious tradition alone, however pious, in the face of saving faith.

sens: The country from which one comes, one's native territory
The city or region where one grew up
The place of origin to which one belongs by birth
G3968.detail:
1. The homeland is primarily the country, the land from which someone originates — the place of their ancestors and birth. It is a geographical and political reality: Jesus returns "to his homeland" (Matthew 13:54), meaning Galilee, the land where he grew up.
2. More concretely, the word often refers to the city or small hometown: when Luke notes that Jesus will not be "well received in his homeland" (Luke 4:24), he speaks of Nazareth where he lived as a child, the place known since childhood.
3. In a figurative or spiritual sense, the homeland becomes the place of belonging, the one toward which one aspires: the patriarchs "desired a better homeland, that is, a heavenly homeland" (Hebrews 11:14), transforming the idea into a spiritual quest for heaven.
G3968.origine: The word comes from "father" (patèr in Greek) and literally means "what belongs to the fathers." It is the poetic feminine of an adjective in Greek that means "of the ancestors." The notion primarily refers to familial and territorial heritage: the land of one's fathers. In ancient Greek, this term contrasts with the life of the foreigner and the traveler, who has no homeland.
G3968.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the New Testament, mainly to speak of Nazareth or Galilee, the region of Jesus' origin. The first three Gospels report the same saying: "A prophet is not without honor except in his homeland" (Matthew 13:57, Mark 6:4, Luke 4:24). This reflects a very concrete reaction: the people of Nazareth do not believe in Jesus precisely because they have known him since childhood and see him as one of their own. John reiterates the idea by saying that the homeland does not believe in the one who comes from it (John 4:44). But the word also takes on a spiritual meaning in Hebrews 11:14, where the homeland becomes heavenly, the hope of faithful believers.
G3968.portee: This word reveals a deep tension of faith: often those who are closest to us — those who have seen us born and grow — have the hardest time believing. Unbelief sometimes comes from familiarity, not ignorance. It is an invitation to examine our own prejudices against those we know too well. At the same time, for the Christian, the passage in Hebrews reminds us that our true homeland is not here on earth: we are pilgrims aspiring to the heavenly homeland, and this perspective should transform our relationship with the present world.

sens: Christian from Rome mentioned in the letter to the Romans
G3969.detail: Patrobas is a Christian living in Rome, likely a member of the young Roman community. Paul greets him by name in his letter to the Romans, indicating that he was well-known or important enough in the assembly to be distinguished from others. He is presented alongside other Christians like Asyncritus and Hermas, and Paul groups him with "the brothers who are with them," suggesting that a small group of believers gathered around him.
G3969.origine: The name Πατροβᾶς (Patrobas) is a Greek compound name, presumably derived from "patro-" (father) and a root indicating life or existence. It was a name used in the Greco-Roman world, particularly among freed slaves or the lower classes. The presence of this name among Paul's greetings indicates that the churches in Rome included people of diverse social status, both free citizens and freedmen.
G3969.emploi: Patrobas appears only once in the Bible, in Romans 16:14, where Paul sends his personal greetings to various members of the Christian community in Rome. He is mentioned by his own name, which was a mark of honor and recognition from the apostle. The context suggests that he was a leader or at least an influential member of a group of believers, as he is named with others and "the brothers who are with them" are associated with these names.

sens: That which comes from the heritage of ancestors
That which is received from generation to generation
That which belongs to ancestral tradition
G3970.detail:
1. The word designates what comes directly from our ancestors, what has been bequeathed to us by them. In 1 Peter 1:18, Peter speaks of the "futile way of life" that Christians have "inherited from their fathers" — the customs, religious or moral practices that each generation received from the previous one without questioning them.
2. It is a transmission that passes from father to son, from generation to generation, forming a continuous chain: what the ancestors practiced and believed becomes the norm for their descendants.
3. The word emphasizes the weight of tradition: the Hebrews had received from their fathers a "futile" way of living (that is, sterile, without real value), a form devoid of meaning — until Christ liberated them through his redemption.
