G3970.origine: The Greek word comes from two elements: "patèr" (father) and "paradidômi" (to transmit, to deliver). The same root is found in "patriarch" or "patronymic." It is a classical Greek formation to say: what has been handed down by the fathers, what is "paternal" in the sense of "coming from the fathers." The central idea is that of transmission: something passes from one person's hands to that of his son.
G3970.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament (1 Peter 1:18). Peter uses it to criticize the tradition inherited from the fathers: it was "futile," meaning hollow, without true substance. The context is that of redemption by the blood of Christ — Peter asserts that we have been freed, not by gold or silver, but by this precious sacrifice. The ancestral tradition that dominated before Christ was merely a spiritual prison, a futile way of living passed down from generation to generation. Peter uses this unique word to mark the break: what came from the fathers, Christ has shattered.
G3970.portee: This word invites every Christian to honestly examine their heritage: what practices, what beliefs received from our fathers or our culture are truly solid, and which are "futile," that is, empty of true meaning? Peter calls us not to cling to tradition for its own sake, but to recognize that only Christ offers true redemption — not the gold or silver of our ancestors, but his shed blood. It is a call to spiritual freedom and a critical look at what we take for granted.

sens: That which comes from the fathers, that which comes from the ancestors
Concerning the tradition, the law, or the customs of previous generations
That which is part of the continuity of a familial and religious heritage received
G3971.detail:
1. The adjective describes what belongs to the fathers, the ancestors: it is what comes from them, what they have transmitted. Paul speaks of "the law of our fathers" (Acts 22:3), meaning the law that previous generations of Israel received and observed.
2. The word emphasizes tradition and heritage: that which has been passed down from father to son. When Paul says "the God of my fathers" (Acts 24:14), he affirms that he worships the same God that his ancestors worshiped, in the continuity of generations.
3. The image is that of a chain: each generation receives from the fathers what it will pass on to its children. In speaking of the "customs of our fathers" (Acts 28:17), Paul shows that he does not oppose Israel's past, but rather that he is part of its continuity.
G3971.origine: The word comes from the root "patēr" (father). The adjective "patrōos" literally means "that which belongs to the father" or "paternal." It is a word formed directly to express what concerns filiation and familial heritage. It often translates in Greek the Hebrew idea of a good or practice that is passed down from one generation to another through the family.
G3971.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in Paul's speeches in Acts. He describes the law, the customs, and the faith of Israel as inheritances passed down by the ancestors. In Acts 22:3, Paul affirms his education at the feet of Gamaliel in the law of his fathers. In Acts 24:14, he claims to serve the God of his fathers, showing that his conversion to Jesus did not break his spiritual lineage. In Acts 28:17, he proclaims to the Jews of Rome that he has done nothing against the customs of his fathers. This word expresses in Paul the awareness of a continuity between the Old Testament and Christianity, rather than a rupture.
G3971.portee: This word invites the believer to consider that the Christian faith does not oppose the biblical heritage, but is rooted in it. It reminds us that the Word of God is heard through the generations, and that respect for the ancestors in faith should help us discern true tradition. For a young Christian, it is a call to root their faith in Scripture and the prayers of previous generations.

sens: The Apostle Paul, apostle to the Gentiles and author of several epistles in the New Testament
A man originally named Saul, a Roman citizen from Tarsus
G3972G.detail:
1. Paul is the great apostle who, after his conversion, brought the Gospel to the Gentile nations. Formerly a persecutor of Christians under the name of Saul, he was turned around by a vision of the risen Christ and became the most zealous missionary of the early Church. Acts shows him preaching in synagogues (Acts 17:2), suffering persecutions (Acts 14:19), and appearing before governors (Acts 25:14). He is also the author of epistles addressed to various churches (1 Corinthians 1:1).
2. Paul was a Jew from Tarsus, an important city in Cilicia, a Roman citizen by birth (Acts 21:39). He had rabbinic education and spoke Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. Although he was initially called Saul, he took the Roman name Paul from his first mission (Acts 13:9).
G3972G.origine: The name "Paulus" is Latin and means "small." In the Greek New Testament, it refers to the one whom Acts first calls Saul (Σαῦλος), the Hebrew name that recalls the king of Israel. The name change marks his transformation: from persecutor to apostle of the Gentiles.
G3972G.emploi: Paul appears 159 times in the New Testament, primarily in the Acts of the Apostles where his missionary journeys are described in detail (Acts 13 to 28). The references show his life as a traveling missionary: he preaches, establishes churches, faces hostility from crowds and authorities (Acts 16:19; 19:15), but also receives encouraging visions (Acts 16:9). Beyond Acts, his name appears as a signature on the epistles he wrote to the Romans, Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, Thessalonians, Timothy, Titus, and Philemon. In 1 Corinthians 1:12, some Christians even claim allegiance to his name, which shows the authority and influence he wields.
G3972G.portee: Paul embodies the radical transformation that the Gospel produces: an enemy of Christ becomes His most faithful servant. His example shows that no one is beyond the grace of God and that an encounter with the risen Christ changes everything. Paul's life, marked by suffering and persecution, inspires Christians to accept the cost of following Jesus. His epistles continue to nourish the faith of churches by explaining how to live the Gospel in concrete circumstances.

sens: Sergius Paulus, proconsul of Cyprus at the time of the apostle
The Apostle Paul, author of several epistles, founder of churches
G3972H.detail:
1. Sergius Paulus was a high-ranking Roman official, proconsul of the island of Cyprus in the first century. In Acts 13:7, he appears as an intelligent man, open to the Gospel, who called for Barnabas and Saul to hear the word of God.
2. The Apostle Paul (formerly called Saul) is one of the twelve apostles and the most important missionary of the New Testament. Born a Jew in Tarsus, a persecutor of Christians, he was transformed by a miraculous encounter with the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus. He then became the great propagator of the Gospel to the Gentiles and the author of thirteen epistles in the New Testament.
G3972H.origine: The name "Paul" comes from the Latin Paulus, which means "small" (from paulus, diminutive of "pau", little). This Latin name was adopted by the apostle, probably after his conversion or during his missions to the Gentiles. It replaces his Hebrew name Saul in the accounts of his missionary journeys.
G3972H.emploi: The word Paulos first refers to Sergius Paulus, proconsul of Cyprus mentioned only once in Acts 13:7, during the first mission of Barnabas and Saul. It then refers to the Apostle Paul, who frequently appears in the Acts of the Apostles and identifies himself as the author of the epistles to the Romans, Corinthians, and other churches. Paul was the greatest missionary of the early Church and the principal teacher of salvation by faith in Christ.

sens: stop, interrupt an action
no longer continue, let go
finish, come to an end
abstain from, refrain from
G3973.detail:
1. In the active and literal sense: to make something cease, to stop or interrupt it. In 1 Peter 3:10, it refers to "ceasing" to speak evil, meaning to refrain from speaking in that way.
2. In the middle sense (which is the most frequent in the New Testament): to cease oneself, to stop one's own action. In Luke 5:4, Jesus "ceases" to speak, he stops in the middle of his discourse. In Acts 5:42, the apostles "did not cease" teaching, they continued tirelessly.
3. To come to an end, to disappear: an action or state that is interrupted definitively. In 1 Corinthians 13:8, prophecies "will cease" and tongues "will cease," they will disappear.
4. With a participle (another action): to cease doing a particular thing, to abandon it. In Acts 20:31, Paul "did not cease" to exhort, he did not stop exhorting. In Colossians 1:9, "we do not cease to pray," we do not stop praying.
G3973.origine: The verb παύω comes from an Indo-European root expressing the idea of stopping, resting. In Hebrew, it often translates כָּלָה (kālāh), which means to accomplish, finish, consume. The word belongs to a rich Greek family: we find παῦλα (pause, rest) and compounds like ἐπαύω (to stop, to cease). The basic image is that of something that stops, that comes to an end.
G3973.emploi: The verb παύω appears fifteen times in the recorded usages, mainly in the Gospel of Luke and in Acts. In Luke 5:4 and 8:24, Jesus ceases to speak or acts to calm the storm. In Acts, the word often returns to describe the tirelessness of the apostles: in 5:42, 20:31, 21:32, we see disciples who "do not cease" to teach or act. The meaning nuances according to the context: voluntary cessation (Acts 13:10), momentary interruption (Luke 5:4), continuous persistence with negation ("did not cease"). In 1 Corinthians 13:8 and Hebrews 10:2, the verb describes the end of temporal realities in the face of eternal love or definitive justice.
G3973.portee: This word speaks to us of perseverance and abandonment. When Paul says "we do not cease to pray," he shows a faith that does not give up, a prayer that perseveres despite obstacles. Conversely, "ceasing to sin" (1 Peter 4:1) calls the believer to break definitively with evil. The word invites us to discern what we must cease (evil, our human efforts) and what we must never cease (prayer, teaching, faith).

sens: Coastal city on the island of Cyprus
G3974.detail: Paphos is an important port city in Cyprus, in the Mediterranean basin. It is where Paul and Barnabas arrive after crossing the island from Salamis during the first missionary journey (Acts 13:6). It is also the port from which they embark to leave Cyprus and go to Perga in Pamphylia (Acts 13:13).
G3974.origine: The name Paphos historically designates one of the oldest cities in the known world, located on the west of Cyprus. It was an important center of pre-Christian worship and a major commercial crossroads on the maritime routes of the eastern Mediterranean.
G3974.emploi: Paphos appears twice in the New Testament, both times in chapter 13 of Acts, which recounts the first missionary journey of Paul and Barnabas. In Acts 13:6, it is in Paphos that they find Bar-Jesus, a false Jewish prophet who has some influence over the proconsul Sergius Paulus. In Acts 13:13, Paphos is the maritime starting point from which Paul and his companions leave Cyprus. These passages show Paphos as a key stop in the expansion of early Christianity into the Mediterranean regions, a place of confrontation between the Gospel and the spiritual powers opposing it.
G3974.portee: Paphos illustrates how the Gospel spread by crossing the major coastal cities of the ancient Mediterranean world. It reminds us that Paul's mission did not respect land borders but unfolded through trade and maritime routes, reaching every important port to proclaim Christ.

sens: To become thick or fat, to grow fat
To become heavy, obtuse, unable to understand
To have a hardened heart, closed to spiritual understanding
G3975.detail:
1. The word first evokes physical thickening: flesh that thickens and fattens. This is the basic image, that of the body becoming fat and heavy.
2. From there, the meaning broadens to intelligence and senses: to become "thick" in spirit means to become obtuse, insensitive to impressions. The heart, hearing, sight lose their sharpness.
3. In the Bible, this hardening mainly applies to the soul: the heart of the people has "become insensitive" (Matthew 13:15, Acts 28:27), unable to see, hear, and understand God's message, closed to conversion.
G3975.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective « pachys » (thick, fat). Its primary image is physical: the thickening of the flesh. Used in the passive (reflexive sense), it describes the result: to become thick. The Hebrew word « shamên » (to become fat, to harden) that it translates in Isaiah 6:10 carries the same double idea: the fattening of the body and the insensitivity of the soul.
G3975.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both in prophetic quotations from the Old Testament. In Matthew 13:15 and Acts 28:27, it is exactly the same verse quoted (Isaiah 6:10): the heart of the people has "become insensitive." The context is one of refusal to listen to the divine message. This hardening is not accidental: it is part of a mysterious design where the repeated refusal to obey leads to a progressive closing of the soul to God's calls.
G3975.portee: This word warns: it is possible for our heart to thicken, to harden gradually through refusal to listen. The Bible does not describe an arbitrary punishment, but a natural consequence of prolonged disobedience. Staying attentive to God's voice, maintaining a tender heart open to His Word, is to protect oneself from this fatal spiritual thickening.

sens: Chain or metal ring fixed around the ankle or foot to restrain a prisoner
Shackle, captivity, servitude
G3976.detail:
1. The word literally designates a chain or iron ring attached to the feet of a prisoner or slave to prevent escape. In Mark 5:4, the demoniac had iron on his feet: despite these restraints, he broke the chains and destroyed the irons, so great was the power of the demon possessing him.
2. Figuratively, the word represents enslavement, spiritual captivity. The iron on the feet symbolizes the slavery of evil that holds and paralyzes: the demon-possessed man in Luke 8:29 was held by the irons as if by an invisible prison, until Jesus freed him.
G3976.origine: The Greek word πέδη comes from a root evoking the foot (πέζα, which means the instep, the arch of the foot). It etymologically designates what hinders the foot. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates Hebrew words designating shackles or instruments of captivity. The term belongs to the vocabulary of chains and bonds, joining words of the same family that all evoke captivity or restriction of movement.
G3976.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the accounts of the demoniac of Gadara (Mark 5:4 and Luke 8:29, which recount the same event). In these two passages, the iron on the feet primarily symbolizes the human attempt to control a possessed man: he was kept chained and ironed to master him. But the demon gave him superhuman strength to break these bonds. Thus, the iron on the feet illustrates the impotence of mere human strength or earthly instruments against the power of evil—only Jesus can truly liberate.
G3976.portee: This image of iron on the feet reminds the reader that true evil is not merely physical or social, but spiritual. Visible shackles are not enough when a wicked force possesses someone from within: only the intervention of Jesus, the Word of God, can break the true chains. It is a call to seek true freedom not in human strength, but in the Lord.

sens: Flat and even terrain
Esplanade where Jesus teaches and heals
G3977.detail:
1. The word designates a flat and even terrain, in contrast to mountains or rugged valleys. It is a solid, horizontal area of land where one can easily stand and move. In Luke 6:17, Jesus "stopped on a plateau" after coming down from the mountain where he had prayed all night: it is an accessible place where a large crowd can gather.
2. By extension, the plateau becomes the place of teaching and healing: Jesus descends there to be at the level of his people, to listen to them and heal them. It is less a spiritual elevation than a physical and concrete closeness to those who suffer.
G3977.origine: The Greek word comes from "plain" (πεδίον) and literally means "of the plain" or "belonging to the plain." It generally translates, in the Greek Old Testament, the Hebrew word for lowlands or plains. The image is that of a smooth surface, without roughness.
G3977.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 6:17. It marks a contrast with the summit of the mountain from which Jesus had just come down: after solitary retreat and prayer, he returns to a level accessible to the crowd. It is the place of Jesus' practical ministry to the sick and the disciples, no longer in solitude, but in public visibility.
G3977.portee: This small topographical detail suggests that Christ does not remain isolated in contemplation: he descends to men, within their reach, to teach and heal them. The plateau, an image of common ground, recalls the incarnation itself — God who lowers himself to us.

sens: To travel by walking on solid ground, as opposed to traveling by sea
To cover a distance by walking rather than sailing
G3978.detail:
1. The word describes the act of traveling by walking on solid ground, as opposed to taking to the sea. In Acts 20:13, Paul "travels the road on foot" while his companions take the boat to Assos: they will meet there, but Paul has chosen the land route rather than the maritime one.
2. More broadly, it means to cover a distance by walking, which implies time and physical effort, unlike the speed of a boat.
G3978.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective πεζός (pezós), which means "on foot" or "terrestrial." It is formed from a root that primarily evokes the notion of walking without the aid of an animal or a boat. The preposition "on foot" in French conveys this idea well: to advance on one's own legs.
G3978.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 20:13. Paul, traveling from Philippi to Assos, deliberately chooses to "travel on foot" rather than immediately board the ship with his companions. This detail shows that the journey could be made by two routes: either by sea (faster) or by land (slower). The usage highlights the concrete choices of early travelers and illustrates the realities of missionary travel.
G3978.portee: This word reminds us that the apostles and early Christians did not hesitate to undertake journeys on foot to serve the Gospel. It is a small detail that humanizes the biblical narrative: behind the great movements of the Church are men who walk, who toil, who make practical choices to continue their mission.

sens: To move by walking, without mount or boat
To oppose a journey by boat, as opposed to maritime travel
To go by land, by road
G3979.detail:
1. The basic meaning is literal: to walk on one's own feet to move. In Matthew 14:13 and Mark 6:33, entire crowds set out on foot to reach Jesus and his disciples — it is a popular movement, at the pace of legs, without special equipment.

2. In the context of Matthew 14:13, where Jesus travels by boat, the contrast is clear: the crowd comes on foot while the disciples depart by sea. It is the opposition between two modes of transport: the boat versus walking on land.

3. In Mark 6:33, we see crowds from several cities rushing on foot to the same place — it is a mass movement, urgent and popular, which underscores the enthusiasm and determination of those who follow Jesus.
G3979.origine: The Greek word comes from πούς (pous), which means "foot." The adverb πεζῇ literally designates the journey "by feet" — that is to say, on foot, as opposed to any other means of transport. It can also refer to land travel in general, opposed to sea travel.
G3979.emploi: The word appears only twice in the provided New Testament, both in Matthew and Mark. In Matthew 14:13, after Jesus learns of John the Baptist's death, he departs by boat to pray alone, while the crowd, upon learning this, follows him on foot to the wilderness — a journey that reveals the ardent desire of the people to join him despite the distance. In Mark 6:33, a similar scene shows people from several cities rushing on foot to reach the place where Jesus and the disciples are heading. In both passages, the adverb emphasizes the contrast between the mode of transport of the disciples (boat) and that of the crowd (walking), highlighting the determination of the multitude.
G3979.portee: This word shows the enthusiasm and commitment of the crowds toward Jesus. Despite the fatigue of walking and the distances, people abandon their cities to follow him — this illustrates the power of his appeal and the spiritual hunger of those who seek him. It is a simple yet powerful reminder that faith sometimes inspires people to make concrete sacrifices.

sens: To submit to one who has authority, to respect their command
To listen to and follow the directives of someone in a position of power
G3980.detail:
1. To obey means primarily to submit to the authority of a person — a magistrate, a leader, God himself — and to do what they command. It is to recognize their right to command and act accordingly. Peter and the apostles express it clearly: "We must obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29), affirming that divine authority takes precedence over any other.
2. The word can also mean "to listen" in the sense of taking into account someone's advice or warnings. When Paul tells the sailors, "You should have listened to me and not set sail from Crete" (Acts 27:21), he refers to obedience to wise words, to advice that should have been followed.
G3980.origine: The word comes from two Greek roots: "peitho" (to persuade, to convince) and "arché" (command, authority). It paints a picture of obedience that results from persuasion, from conviction — one obeys because one is convinced that the one commanding has the right and wisdom to do so. It is a thoughtful obedience, not a mere mechanical submission.
G3980.emploi: This verb appears four times in the New Testament, always in the context of submission to authority. Three times in Acts: Peter asserts that we must obey God (5:29), the Spirit is given to those who obey God (5:32), and Paul advises the sailors to listen to him to avoid disaster (27:21). Once in Paul's letter to Titus (3:1), where he exhorts Christians to obey magistrates and civil authorities. The word is therefore used in relation to divine authority and earthly authorities.
G3980.portee: This word raises the fundamental question for Christians: to whom do we ultimately obey? Scripture teaches that obedience to God takes precedence over any other human authority, but also that we must respect established authorities. It is a fruitful tension: Christian obedience is not anarchic, but recognizes God's supremacy. It calls for a maturity of faith: to obey not out of fear, but because one is convinced that the one we listen to is trustworthy.

sens: Having the ability to convince or persuade someone
Relying on eloquence or the art of speaking well rather than on truth or force
G3981.detail:
1. The word describes what is capable of convincing the listener, what has the power to lead someone to believe or act. It is the art of presenting things well so that they seem true and attract adherence. In 1 Corinthians 2:4, Paul speaks of "persuasive words of wisdom" — that is, the beautiful speeches of the wise of the world that aim to impress and convince through their eloquence.
2. The word carries a critical nuance: it designates a persuasion that relies on rhetorical technique, rhetorical skill, rather than on the power of truth itself. Paul contrasts these "persuasive words" with "a demonstration of Spirit and power" — showing that true persuasion comes not from beautiful human speech, but from the action of God.
G3981.origine: The word comes from the verb πείθω (peithô), which means "to persuade," "to convince," "to lead to believe." It is related to the Greek root that evokes the idea of being led or convinced. Paul uses this rare adjectival form to criticize the rhetorical wisdom of the pagan world, in contrast to divine power.
G3981.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 2:4. Paul has just reminded that he did not come to Corinth "with excellence of speech or wisdom" (verse 1): he explains here that his preaching did not rely on the "persuasive words of wisdom," that is, on the rhetorical eloquence that the Greeks admired. Instead, his message was accompanied by signs, wonders, and the power of the Holy Spirit. This context reveals that Paul values the manifestation of divine power more than rhetorical skill.
G3981.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on what truly underpins their faith: beautiful human words and the wisdom of the world, or the transformative power of God? For the Christian, it reminds that the Gospel does not need elaborate persuasion techniques: its strength comes from the Holy Spirit who works in hearts. It is an exhortation to seek authenticity rather than appearance, and to trust in the power of God rather than the artifices of human rhetoric.

sens: Convince someone through words to accept or do something
Have confidence in someone or something, rely on it
Be convinced of the truth of something, believe firmly
Obey someone, be led by them
G3982.detail:
1. The most common meaning is to convince by persuasion: it is trying to gain someone's adherence through speech and argumentation. Matthew 27:20 shows the religious leaders persuading the crowd to demand the death of Jesus; Acts 19:26 recounts how Paul persuaded the inhabitants of Asia that idols are not really gods.
2. The word can also mean to have confidence in or rely on something or someone, to be assured of their reliability. In Philippians 3:4, Paul says he could put confidence in the flesh, that is, rely on his natural advantages or merits.
3. In the passive voice, it means to be convinced, to firmly believe in something. Romans 8:38 expresses this unwavering conviction: Paul is persuaded that no power can separate him from the love of Christ.
4. The word also means to listen and obey, to be led by someone: in Galatians 5:7, being turned away from the right path means ceasing to listen to the truth; in Hebrews 13:17, believers must obey their leaders.
G3982.origine: The Greek word peithô comes from an ancient root that evokes the idea of placing trust or being persuaded. In Hebrew, it often translates the verb בָּטַח (batah), which means to rely on, to have confidence, to lean on. The family of the word includes derivatives like peitheia (persuasion) and the name Peithô, which referred in Greek mythology to the goddess of persuasion. This link between persuasion and trust shows that for the ancients, being persuaded is to trust, and to trust is to be persuaded.
G3982.emploi: The verb peithô appears 54 times in the New Testament, mostly in Acts and Paul's epistles. In Acts, it often describes the action of trying to convince: Paul persuades the synagogues (Acts 18:4), the religious leaders try to persuade the crowd against Jesus. In the Pauline epistles, the word gradually shifts from the meaning of persuading to that of trusting and believing: in Philippians, Paul repeatedly expresses that he is assured, confident in the Lord. The passive voice (to be persuaded, to believe) is common, especially to express a firmly established conviction. The word also includes the idea of obeying (Hebrews 13:17), as listening to someone and obeying them is ultimately being persuaded by them.
G3982.portee: This word illuminates the power of speech and conviction in the Christian life. It shows that faith is not a blind impulse but an intelligent adherence, a heart's persuasion. For the believer, "being persuaded" that God keeps His promises means living in trust and obedience. The word also invites reflection on what truly persuades us: are we persuaded by the lies of the world or by the truth of the Gospel? Trusting in Christ is this deep persuasion that we can abandon ourselves to Him.

sens: To feel the physical sensation of lack of food
To be in need, deprived of necessary things
To intensely desire something
To spiritually aspire to righteousness and to God
G3983.detail:
1. To hunger primarily designates the physical sensation of the stomach crying out for food, the urgent need to eat. Jesus, after forty days of fasting, "was hungry" (Luke 4:2): it is the physical reality of hunger that affects Him.
2. The word extends to a broader material need: to be hungry means to be in want, lacking what is necessary. David and his men "were hungry" (Mark 2:25): they were on the run, without resources.
3. To hunger can also mean to desire intensely: to aspire to something as one aspires to food when hungry. The image of hunger expresses ardent desire.
4. Spiritually, to hunger or thirst for righteousness (Matthew 5:6) means to passionately desire it, to aspire with all one's being, just as one longs to eat when starving. It is a soul's appetite for what is just and holy.
G3983.origine: The word comes from a Greek root that expresses the sensation of deprivation. In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew word meaning "to hunger." It is a simple and direct verb, without complex derivatives: it simply states the elementary experience of lack.
G3983.emploi: The word appears 23 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels. It first describes concrete situations: Jesus fasting for forty days (Matthew 4:2, Luke 4:2), the hungry disciples in the fields (Matthew 12:1, Mark 2:25), the fig tree without fruit that "was hungry," meaning it was barren (Mark 11:12). Then it becomes a theme in Jesus' teaching: blessed are those who hunger for righteousness (Matthew 5:6), and especially a criterion of the Last Judgment — "Did you see someone who was hungry?" (Matthew 25:35-44). Revelation promises that the redeemed will no longer hunger (Revelation 7:16). Finally, John 6:35 uses the word figuratively: whoever believes in Jesus will never hunger in the deep sense.
G3983.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus experienced physical need just like us: His hunger was not simulated, it was real and human. But the Bible makes hunger — both physical and spiritual — a call: to feed those who are hungry is to serve Jesus Himself; and to hunger for righteousness is the attitude of the believer who ardently desires holiness. This humble word places us before two responsibilities: to empathize with the material needs of others, and to cultivate a spiritual appetite for God.

sens: Trial, action of testing
Experience gained through practice
Risk taken by venturing into the unknown
G3984.detail:
1. The word denotes the action of making an attempt, trying something to verify the outcome. It is to test, to seek to achieve a goal without certainty of the result. In Hebrews 11:29, the Egyptians make an attempt to cross the Red Sea as the Israelites did, but fail: they try without having the faith that saves.
2. The word can also mean the experience, the know-how acquired through trying, through practice. It is the result of repeated attempts, the knowledge gained from testing.
3. By extension, it is the trial itself, the risk one takes when embarking on something unknown or difficult — like the persecutions and sufferings that believers have endured (Hebrews 11:36).
G3984.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb πειράω (peiráô), which means "to try, to attempt, to test." This family of words evokes the idea of verifying the solidity of something, as one tests a metal in fire. In Hebrew, this term often translates נָסָה (nasáh) and מַסָּה (massáh), which share the same idea of trial and attempt. It is a concrete word that speaks of action.
G3984.emploi: The word πεῖρα appears twice in the New Testament, only in Hebrews 11. In verse 29, it describes the attempt of the Egyptians to cross the Red Sea — a failed attempt, unlike that of the Israelites guided by faith. In verse 36, in the passage of the "cloud of witnesses," the word also encompasses the trials and persecutions endured by the saints of the Old Testament: mockeries, chains, imprisonments. In all cases, it is an action or an experience that reveals faith or the absence of faith.
G3984.portee: This word reminds the believer that faith is measured not by caution or human calculation, but by bold action in trust towards God. The Egyptians attempted to do what only faith could accomplish; the saints of the Old Testament endured attempts at destruction, but it was their faithfulness that mattered. For the reader, it is an exhortation not to fear the trial, but to go through it with faith.

sens: To put to the test, to try
To seek to lead into sin
To doubt, to challenge, to defy
To test through difficulties or sufferings
G3985G.detail:
1. To tempt someone is primarily to put them to the test to verify their quality, solidity, or faithfulness — like testing a weapon before battle. God tests Abraham by asking him to sacrifice his son (Genesis 22:1): it is not to lose him, but to see his faith. Jesus was also tested (Hebrews 2:18), suffering as we do to better help us.
2. To tempt someone also means to incite them to evil, to push them to sin. This is what the devil tries to do with Jesus in the desert (Matthew 4:1): to divert him from his path. Satan tempts us when he offers us sin (1 Corinthians 7:5), playing on our weaknesses.
3. To tempt someone can also mean to put them in difficulty through tricky questions or challenges, to embarrass or trap them. The Pharisees tempted Jesus by asking him malicious questions.
4. To tempt also means to allow or send trials — sufferings or tribulations — to strengthen faith. God does not abandon us in these temptations (1 Corinthians 10:13), but gives us the strength to resist them.
G3985G.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to make an attempt," "to put to the test." In Hebrew, נָסָה (nassa) carries both meanings: to test and also to incite to evil. The Greek πειράζω borrows from Hebrew this dual meaning, reflecting a truth: the same trial can strengthen faith or break it, depending on how one receives it. Related words include δοκιμάζω (dokimazō, "to test by judging"), but πειράζω emphasizes more the process of the trial itself.
G3985G.emploi: The verb πειράζω appears twelve times in the New Testament, mostly in the epistles and the Gospels. Matthew and Mark describe the temptation of Jesus in the desert by Satan (Matthew 4:1, Mark 1:13): a real trial where Jesus confronts evil. The apostles use the word to speak of the temptations that await Christians (1 Corinthians 7:5, Galatians 6:1): these are trials where faith can waver. James clearly poses the question of meaning: Does God tempt to sin (James 1:13)? No — that is the role of the devil and our own desires. But God allows or sends tribulations to strengthen us (Hebrews 2:18, 1 Corinthians 10:13). The meaning thus varies: temptation to evil (the role of the devil), temptation to good or to pray (the role of God).
G3985G.portee: Understanding this distinction changes everything for the Christian. When you go through a trial or when you feel an urge to sin, you must ask: where does this temptation come from? If it is an incitement to evil, it does not come from God (James 1:13). But if it is a difficulty, a loss, an illness, God may allow it to strengthen your faith. Above all, Jesus was tempted like you (Hebrews 4:15), and he stood firm: you never face the trial alone. This is the freedom of the Christian: to recognize that God never pushes us to evil, but gives us the strength to resist temptations and to grow in faith through trials.

sens: Put to the test, submit to a test to know the quality or strength of something
Tempt someone, seek to lead them to evil or sin
Try to trap someone with questions or traps, with the aim of compromising them
Submit to an affliction or difficulty sent by God to test faith
G3985H.detail:
1. The broadest meaning is to "put to the test": to verify the nature or strength of someone or something through a test. Jesus said to his disciples: "He said this to test him, for he knew what he was going to do" (John 6:6), meaning he wanted to see how they would react to the lack of food.
2. The verb also means "to tempt" in a moral sense: to seek to lead someone toward evil or sin. James warns: "Let no one say when he is tempted, 'I am tempted by God'" (James 1:13), for God does not lead anyone to evil. This is primarily the role of the devil, who "tempts" believers to make them fall.
3. In the Gospels, the verb often describes the attempts of religious leaders to "test" Jesus with tricky questions: "The Pharisees and Sadducees approached Jesus and, to test him, asked him to show them a sign from heaven" (Matthew 16:1). They hoped to catch him in a fault or discredit him.
4. Finally, to test means "to submit to an affliction" sent by God to test and strengthen faith. This is why we speak of the "trials" that God sends to believers, not to destroy them, but to strengthen them: "No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man; God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability" (1 Corinthians 10:13).
G3985H.origine: The Greek word πειράζω comes from an ancient root related to the idea of "seeking," "trying." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it often translates the verb נָסָה (nasa), which means "to test." This Hebrew verb is used to describe how God tests Abraham's faith by asking him to sacrifice his son (Genesis 22:1), or how the people "tempt" God in the desert through their unbelief. The notion of trial, test, and questioning is at the heart of the word.
G3985H.emploi: The verb πειράζω appears 22 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) and in the epistles. Its meaning varies according to the context. In the Gospels, it describes the attempts of Jesus' adversaries (Pharisees, Sadducees) who question him to trap him (Matthew 16:1, 22:35; Mark 12:15). In Paul and James, the verb distinguishes two sources of temptation: God who "tests" or "trials" the faith of believers to strengthen it (1 Corinthians 10:13, Hebrews 11:17), and the devil who "tempts" believers to lead them into sin (1 Thessalonians 3:5). This distinction is crucial: testing can come from God, but "tempting to evil" always comes from the evil one.
G3985H.portee: This word helps the believer understand the difference between the trial that God allows (to strengthen faith) and the temptation to evil (which comes from the devil). It also assures that God does not abandon us in the face of difficulties: he tests us to make us stronger and more faithful. Knowing the exact meaning of "to test" allows us to see that suffering is not always punishment, but sometimes a school of faith.

sens: Seek to verify, to test something or someone
Try to do something
Put to the test to seduce toward evil
Test through difficulties or sufferings
G3985I.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to seek to test, to verify — as one tests something to know its value or quality. Jesus questions the crowd to verify their faith (John 6:6); God tests Abraham to prove his trust (Genesis 22:1).
2. To try to do something, with the sense of an attempt: the apostles "attempted" to enter Bithynia (Acts 16:7), they were striving to go there.
3. To seek to lead someone toward evil, to seduce them to sin — this is the sense of the devil who tempts Jesus (Matthew 4:1), or that of the one who "attempted" to profane the temple (Acts 24:6).
4. To test someone through difficulties, sufferings, obstacles sent or allowed by God to strengthen faith: God allows believers to be tested to reinforce their trust (Hebrews 2:18).
G3985I.origine: The word comes from an ancient Greek root meaning "to make an attempt, to test." It corresponds in Hebrew to the verb נָסָה (nassa), which carries the same meanings: to test, to try, to put to the test. Greek and Hebrew share this same image: that of verifying something, as one tests a metal to know its quality. The context determines whether the trial comes from God (to strengthen) or from the devil (to lead away from good).
G3985I.emploi: The word appears about forty times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and the epistles. It has two main meanings: to seek to test (also: to try, to undertake), and to seduce toward evil. The Gospels use it frequently for the attempts of Jesus' adversaries — the Pharisees "tempted" him by asking tricky questions (Matthew 16:1, Mark 8:11). The epistles mainly discuss the temptations of the devil (Matthew 4:1, Luke 4:2) or the trials that God allows believers (Hebrews 2:18, 4:15). The word can also simply mean "to try" (Acts 16:7: "attempted to enter"). James emphasizes that God does not tempt anyone to evil (James 1:13).
G3985I.portee: This word speaks to us of two important realities: first, God tests our faith to strengthen it, and he remains with us in these trials; secondly, the devil seeks to lead us toward evil, but Jesus was tested like us and can help us (Hebrews 4:15). Understanding this word helps us distinguish what comes from God (who tests to strengthen) and what comes from the adversary (who would seduce to lead astray).

sens: Trial, test intended to assess someone's quality or resilience
Difficulty or affliction sent by God to test faith
Solicitation to evil, incitement to sin
Moment of weakness in the face of the desire to sin
G3986G.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a trial or test that measures someone's strength — just as the quality of a metal is tested. It is an experience meant to reveal what one truly is.
2. In the Bible, the afflictions and difficulties that God allows (poverty, illness, persecution) are often called temptations, not to push us toward evil, but to strengthen our faith and trust in Him. Jesus prays: "deliver us from temptation" (Matthew 6:13), asking God to protect us from moments when our trust wavers.
3. Temptation can also mean an active solicitation to sin — someone or something pushes us to do evil. Thus, the devil tempted Jesus "in all these ways" (Luke 4:13) to make Him fall.
4. More broadly, it is the state of weakness where one risks falling into sin, when our carnal desires or fears dominate us. Paul warns Timothy that "the love of money is a root of all evils" (1 Timothy 6:9), as it exposes one to the risk of sinning.
G3986G.origine: The word comes from the verb "peirazô" (to tempt, to test), which originally has the simple meaning of trying or testing. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it often translates "massah" (trial, test), particularly in the story of the people of Israel in the desert — a time when God tests the faith of His people. The word always retains this idea of a trial, whether it comes from God to strengthen us, or from our own weakness that exposes us to evil.
G3986G.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the Segond, mainly in the Gospels and the epistles. It encompasses two distinct realities depending on the context. On one hand, the afflictions or difficulties that God uses to test and strengthen faith: Jesus teaches to pray not to enter into temptation, meaning that God preserves us in critical moments when our trust falters (Matthew 6:13, Luke 11:4, Luke 22:40). On the other hand, the solicitation to sin itself: the devil "tempts" Jesus (Luke 4:13), and Paul warns against desires that expose us to sin (1 Corinthians 10:13, 1 Timothy 6:9). Temptation is never presented as coming from God in the sense that He wants us to sin, but as an inevitable reality of earthly existence.
G3986G.portee: This word reminds Christians that trials are not useless punishments: they test and strengthen us. It also teaches us that praying "lead us not into temptation" does not mean asking God to abolish evil, but to give us the strength not to succumb when we are confronted with it. The distinction between the trial that builds up and the solicitation to evil that brings us down is central to understanding how God acts and how we must resist.

sens: Test, experience intended to highlight the quality or reality of something
Difficulty, adversity, or suffering sent by God to strengthen faith
Solicitation to sin, push toward evil
Testing or provocation directed at God
G3986H.detail:
1. In the broadest sense, it is an experience, a test that shows what is true and authentic — like when one tests a metal to know its purity.

2. In the Bible, it is often a difficulty or suffering that God allows (or even sends) to test and strengthen the faith of believers. In Galatians 4:14, Paul refers to his physical illness as a "trial" that revealed the true compassion of the Galatians; in James 1:2, the apostle exhorts believers to see various trials as a joy, because they produce perseverance.

3. But the word also refers to temptation in the sense of evil — the attraction to sin, the solicitation to abandon God. In Luke 8:13, those who "fall away in the time of temptation" are tempted to abandon their faith when difficulties arise.

4. It can finally mean a provocation directed at God, when man tests God by doubting His faithfulness — as Hebrews 3:8 recalls the day when Israel rebelled and tempted God in the desert.
G3986H.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb "peirazô" which means to try, to tempt, to test. It originally has the neutral sense of "experience" (as in sciences); then it takes on a moral hue: to test someone to see if they are faithful, or to solicit them to evil. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew word "massah," which literally means "trial" and historically refers to the desert where Israel tested God (Exodus 17:7, Psalms 95:8-9).
G3986H.emploi: The word appears eleven times in the New Testament, mainly in the epistles (James, Peter, Hebrews) and in the Gospels (particularly Luke). It has two main shades. First, the "trial" in the positive sense: a difficulty or suffering sent by God that tests and purifies faith (James 1:2, 1 Peter 1:6, 4:12); this meaning is also found in the account of the Temptation of Jesus (Luke 4:13), where Jesus faces the devil's challenge without wavering. Secondly, the "temptation" in the sense of sin: the attraction to evil, as in Luke 8:13 or 1 Corinthians 10:13, where Paul speaks of not succumbing to temptation. Finally, in Hebrews 3:8, the word evokes provocation, when Israel tested God's patience in the desert.
G3986H.portee: For the believer, this word gives meaning to suffering: trials are not accidents, but opportunities to grow in faith and show that our attachment to God is sincere. At the same time, the word warns us that the temptation to sin is real and always present — not to condemn us, but to keep us vigilant and remind us that we can rely on God's faithfulness, who "will not allow you to be tempted beyond your strength" (1 Corinthians 10:13).

sens: To try to do something, to undertake an action
To seek to achieve a goal, even if difficult or risky
G3987.detail:
1. The word expresses the action of trying or attempting something: one strives to do it, one takes the initiative. In Acts 26:21, Paul recounts that the Jews "attempted to kill me" — meaning they tried, they attempted to kill him, they took action to achieve it.
2. More broadly, this verb evokes a serious attempt, a genuine effort to reach a goal. The word implies that one does not remain passive, but acts or undertakes something, whether the outcome is certain or not.
G3987.origine: This Greek verb comes from a root that fundamentally means "to test" or "to try." It often appears in the Greek Old Testament to translate a Hebrew word meaning "to test" or "to try." The form we see here is the middle voice (the subject acts for itself), which was common in ancient Greek and does not require a special translation: it retains the same meaning.
G3987.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, specifically in the passage of Acts 26:21. Paul, testifying before King Agrippa, reports how the Jews seized him in the temple and attempted to kill him. The word "to attempt" emphasizes that there was an attempt, a concrete action, even if it did not succeed. It is a rather rare word in the New Testament, but it appears in the Greek Old Testament with the same meaning of trying or testing.
G3987.portee: This verb reminds the reader that the intentions of Paul's adversaries were serious and threatening: they did not just think evil, they acted. For the Christian, it is an illustration of the reality of persecution: Paul did not imagine the danger, he lived it. It also invites reflection on our own commitment: where do we attempt to go, what are we really seeking to accomplish?

sens: The act of persuading, convincing someone by words
Anything that inclines the mind toward a conviction or action
The persuasive effect of a doctrine or a word
G3988.detail:
1. The word refers to the act of persuading, that is, convincing someone and winning them to one's opinion. It is the work of one who speaks forcefully to lead another to believe or act. In Galatians 5:8, Paul rejects an "influence" that would divert Christians from the truth: someone is trying to persuade them to reject the freedom in Christ.

2. The term extends to any power of conviction, to anything that carries adherence: a word, a doctrine, an idea that makes you lean one way rather than the other. It is less about the action than the persuasive weight itself, the capacity to carry conviction.

3. In Galatians 5:8, Paul speaks of an "influence" that does not come from God: it is a seductive power, a deceptive persuasion that claims to guide but actually leads away from the truth. It is a spiritual force at play in the life of the Church.
G3988.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "peitho" (πείθω), which means to persuade, convince, or also to trust, believe. In the Hebrew of the Greek Old Testament, this verb often translates "batah," which means to have confidence, to rely on. The noun "peismonè" (πεισμονή) is formed from the verb to describe the act or state of persuasion, like the word that acts on the mind of a listener.
G3988.emploi: The word appears only once in the preserved New Testament, in Galatians 5:8. Paul uses it at the moment when he rebukes the Galatians who are being led away from the truth of the Gospel: someone is persuading them to abandon the freedom in Christ to return to the Law. This unique occurrence shows that the word denotes a spiritual persuasive force, dangerous because it comes from one who troubles the churches, not from God. The context indicates that this "influence" is human, deceptive, and contrary to God's call to freedom and faith.
G3988.portee: This word reminds Christians to discern the voices that press upon them, not to passively be convinced by every seductive influence, especially in matters of faith. It invites them to ask: where does this persuasion come from? Does it come from God or from a human or evil power? It teaches spiritual vigilance in a world full of words that seek to divert from the path of the Gospel.

sens: The deep part of the sea, the marine abyss
The body of water itself, considered as traversable
G3989.detail:
1. The bottom of the sea refers to the marine depth, the abyss: this is the most dramatic sense of the word. Jesus speaks of it when he says it would be better to "be thrown into the bottom of the sea" for one who causes a little child to stumble (Matthew 18:6) — an image of terrible judgment, of what engulfs and annihilates.
2. The word can also simply refer to the sea as a navigable expanse that one crosses: thus, Luke recounts that Paul and his companions "cross the sea" of Cilicia and Pamphylia (Acts 27:5) — the sea, here, is the space to be traversed, without emphasis on depth, but rather on the journey.
G3989.origine: The Greek word pelagos (πέλαγος) comes from an ancient root meaning the open and vast space, the liquid plain. It is close to the root of "plain" in Greek and evokes an expanse without limits. Unlike "thalassa" (θάλασσα), which is the common word for "sea," pelagos emphasizes depth, immensity, and sometimes danger — it is the aspect of "abyss" rather than "shore" or "navigation."
G3989.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus uses it to speak of judgment: throwing someone to the bottom of the sea means condemning them to disappear, without hope. In Acts, Luke uses it in the more neutral sense of "sea" that one crosses during a maritime journey. The context thus changes the tone: sometimes it is a fearsome abyss (in a figurative and theological sense), sometimes it is simply the mass of water faced during a crossing.
G3989.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, the sea and the abyss are never neutral: they can symbolize judgment, separation from God, or the obstacle to overcome to follow Jesus. Understanding this symbolic charge helps the reader grasp how Jesus speaks of future punishment and why storms, in biblical accounts, are so laden with spiritual meaning.

sens: To cut off the head with an axe or a sharp instrument
To execute someone by beheading
G3990.detail:
1. The word evokes the concrete image of cutting, severing: using an axe or sword to separate the head from the body. It is a brutal and irreversible action, that of executioners.
2. In the New Testament, the verb is used to describe capital punishment by decapitation: John the Baptist was beheaded (Matthew 14:10), and in Revelation, John sees the souls of those who were "beheaded for the testimony of Jesus" (Revelation 20:4). It is the fate of martyrs and enemies of Roman power.
G3990.origine: The verb comes from the Greek noun πέλεκυς (pélékus), which means "axe" or "hatchet" (a weapon of war). The verb formed from this noun literally means "to strike with an axe." In Hebrew, the corresponding word is קַטַל (qatal), "to cut, to kill." This image of the axe recalls that decapitation was a form of execution practiced in antiquity, both by the Romans and the Greeks.
G3990.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament: in Revelation 20:4, where John describes his heavenly vision of the martyrs. He speaks of the souls of those who were "beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God." It is thus a word specifically used to evoke the fate of Christians persecuted by Roman power in the early centuries, who suffered this form of execution for refusing to renounce their faith.
G3990.portee: This word reminds the reader that the early Christians paid the price for their faith through persecution, some even unto death. Revelation, by naming what was done to them, honors their sacrifice and assures that God has not forgotten their faithfulness: "They came to life, and they reigned with Christ for a thousand years." It is a call to steadfastness in persecution and a promise of redemption.

sens: That which comes after four others in a sequence
Ordinal rank corresponding to the number five
G3991.detail:
1. The word designates what occupies the fifth place in an ordered series. In Revelation, John first sees four seals opened, then the fifth: "When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain" (Revelation 6:9). Similarly, four angels sound the trumpet before the fifth, which triggers terrible events (Revelation 9:1). It is a simple indication of a position in an enumeration.
2. In the description of the heavenly Jerusalem, the precious stones are listed in order: "the fifth of sardonyx, the sixth of sardius" (Revelation 21:20). The word here purely expresses the numerical rank, without any particular connotation beyond counting.
G3991.origine: The Greek word πέμπτος comes from the root πέμπ- which means "five" (related to the number 5, πέντε). It is the regular ordinal adjective formed from this number, allowing the transition from cardinal ("five") to ordinal ("the fifth"). In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew חֲמִישִׁי (hamichī) which has exactly the same meaning and function.
G3991.emploi: The word πέμπτος appears only four times in the New Testament, all in Revelation. John systematically uses it to designate elements of a sequence: the fifth seal (Revelation 6:9), the fifth angel with the trumpets (Revelation 9:1), the fifth angel with the bowls of wrath (Revelation 16:10), and the fifth foundation stone of the heavenly Jerusalem (Revelation 21:20). In each case, the order matters: it marks a progression in the apocalyptic vision, where each step brings new events or new elements. The word is purely technical and ordinal, without emotional or moral nuance.
G3991.portee: This word invites the reader to follow the order of John's visions and not to neglect it. In Revelation, the progression of the seals, trumpets, and bowls is not arbitrary: each step has a specific eschatological meaning. Recognizing the "fifth" as such helps to grasp the structure and unfolding of God's plan in the last days. It also reminds us that God acts in order and wisdom, even in the terrifying events of the end.

sens: To make someone or something depart to a place or person
To entrust a mission to someone
To charge someone with a word, a message
To dispatch someone to a person
To direct, orient towards a goal
G3992.detail:
1. The simplest meaning: to make someone or something leave one place to arrive elsewhere. It is the material action of sending. Herod "sends" the Magi to Bethlehem to seek Jesus (Matthew 2:8). When the owner of the vineyard "sends" his servants, he dispatches them to his estate (Luke 20:11, 20:12).

2. To entrust someone with a task, a particular responsibility. Paul "sends" Timothy to the Philippians not just for him to travel, but to accomplish a mission among them (Philippians 2:19).

3. To charge someone to carry a message, a word. It is to send someone to "say" something. Jesus "sends" John the Baptist through his disciples to ask him if he is the one who is to come (Luke 7:19: they come to "tell" him what Jesus has sent to say).

4. To dispatch someone expressly to a person, with insistence or urgency. The Asiarchs "send" to Paul to urge him not to go to the theater (Acts 19:31): they do so with intention and care.

5. Particularly in the Gospel of John, being "sent" by God means having received a divine mission, being delegated by God to accomplish his work. Jesus says that whoever receives him receives the one who "sent" him (John 14:24) — it is to recognize that Jesus comes from the Father with his authority.
G3992.origine: The Greek verb πέμπω comes from a root that expresses the action of putting in motion, of making depart. In Hebrew, it mainly translates שָׁלַח (shalakh), which literally means "to send, dispatch." This verb belongs to the family of words concerning mission and sending: this same idea is found in the compounds ἀποστέλλω (apostello, "to send on a mission") and its variants. The biblical notion of "sending" is inseparable from that of delegation and authority: the one who sends exercises authority over the one who is sent.
G3992.emploi: The verb πέμπω appears 78 times in the New Testament. It is used generally for the action of sending someone (Matthew 2:8: Herod sends the Magi), or to send a message by someone (Luke 7:19: John has his disciples send a question). But it is especially in the Gospel of John that the word acquires a theological depth: Jesus is constantly presented as "sent by the Father" (John 7:18, 14:24, 20:21). This nuance of meaning — being sent = having a divine mission — is characteristic of John and distinguishes πέμπω from the purely practical uses found elsewhere. Acts and the epistles use the verb mainly for the concrete sending of messengers or aid (Acts 19:31; Philippians 2:28; Acts 11:29).
G3992.portee: To send someone in the Bible is to clothe them with a mission and authority. When Jesus says he is "sent by the Father," he affirms that all he does comes from the Father and that the Father acts in him. For the Christian, understanding that Jesus is the Father's Sent One is to recognize his divine authority and the source of his message. It also invites reflection on how God "sends us": is every Christian aware that they have a mission, that they do not live for themselves, but as someone whom God has delegated to testify of his grace?

sens: one who does not have enough to live and must work with their hands to survive
a poor person, lacking resources
one who lacks the essentials
G3993.detail:
1. The word designates someone who earns their daily bread by working with their hands — a laborer, a day laborer without reserves. It is an active poverty, that of someone who must toil every day to eat, different from begging. Paul cites this word in 2 Corinthians 9:9 to show that whoever shows generosity towards these poor workers fulfills God's justice.
2. More broadly, it refers to any man or woman who lacks essential resources and depends on their work or the help of others to survive. The Pauline context of giving (2 Corinthians 9) emphasizes the duty of the affluent Christian to provide for the needs of these needy individuals.
G3993.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning "to work, to toil for a living." It designates one who must "toil" (πένεσθαι) for their daily bread. Ancient Greek distinguishes this term from πτωχός ("beggar"), which describes a more extreme poverty: the needy works, the beggar cannot. The Hebrew Bible uses several words for "poor" (אֶבְיוֹן, עָנִי, דַּל), all rendered by this Greek term when the Greek Old Testament translates these social realities.
G3993.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 9:9, where Paul cites Psalm 112:9 to encourage the generosity of the Corinthians. It is noteworthy that Paul elsewhere prefers the term πτωχός ("poor," "beggar") to speak of the needy in the Church. The uniqueness of this usage and its context of biblical citation highlight that the apostle draws from Hebrew Scripture to ground the exhortation to share with the needy.
G3993.portee: This word reminds us that Christian charity is directed towards those who toil to live, without the minimum necessary. It challenges every affluent believer regarding their concrete duty to support not only beggars but also poor workers who do not earn enough to subsist with dignity. It is a biblical call to social justice rooted in compassion.

sens: Mother of the husband or wife (wife of the husband's father, or mother of the husband)
G3994.detail: 1. Mother-in-law refers to the mother of the husband or wife — this is primarily illustrated in the Gospels through the example of Simon (Peter)'s mother-in-law, who suffered from a fever and whom Jesus healed (Matthew 8:14, Mark 1:30, Luke 4:38). The word describes a familial relationship by marriage, not by blood. Jesus also uses it to show that his message will cause tensions even within families, between mother-in-law and daughter-in-law (Luke 12:53, Matthew 10:35) — a sign that the Gospel creates a rupture that transcends ordinary familial ties.
G3994.origine: The Greek word πενθερά comes from a root denoting kinship by marriage. It translates the Hebrew חֲמוֹת (hamot) from the Old Testament. The construction of the word in Greek shows a relationship of in-laws, distinct from direct blood ties.
G3994.emploi: The word appears only in the four Gospels, five times in total. Three passages recount the healing of Peter's mother-in-law by Jesus (Matthew 8:14, Mark 1:30, Luke 4:38) — a discreet miracle but revealing of Jesus' power over illness and his compassion. Two other passages (Matthew 10:35 and Luke 12:53) use the mother-in-law as an example of familial ties that the Gospel will challenge: families will be divided by commitment to Jesus. The word remains simple, without theological nuance, but the context makes it a point of tension.
G3994.portee: This silent mother-in-law becomes a symbol of two truths: first, Jesus cares about the ordinary aspects of life — the fever of an elderly woman deserves his healing. Second, following Jesus may require choosing against familial ties themselves. The contrast between the healed mother-in-law in Matthew 8 and the divided mother-in-law in Luke 12 reveals Jesus' dual action: he heals and he separates.

sens: The father of the spouse, particularly the father of the married woman
The one whose daughter has been married
G3995.detail:
1. The father-in-law is the father of the one whom one has married. It is a kinship created by marriage. John 18:13 shows this with Annas, who was the father-in-law of Caiaphas: Annas had a daughter married to Caiaphas, making him the father of his son-in-law.
2. This term also more broadly designates any man related to someone by this type of familial bond. The relationship of father-in-law to son-in-law or daughter-in-law is important in biblical social life, as it unites two families.
G3995.origine: The Greek word pentheros comes from a root that evokes the alliance or bond formed by marriage. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses the word חָם (ham) to refer to the father-in-law, notably the father of the wife. This kinship by marriage, distinct from blood kinship, has a well-defined place in law and family life.
G3995.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament in Greek, in John 18:13. It is used to describe the relationship between Annas and Caiaphas at the time of Jesus' trial: Annas was the father-in-law of the acting high priest. This context shows that the bond of in-law kinship was recognized legally and socially, as it is cited as an important fact in the relationship between these two Jewish religious figures.
G3995.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus was presented to the religious authorities according to ties of power and family. The mention of the father-in-law emphasizes how religious and political responsibilities were intertwined through familial bonds. For the believer, it is a reminder that even in the midst of the events of Jesus' trial, God knew and saw these human structures.

sens: To feel sadness, sorrow in the face of misfortune, loss, or mourning
To shed tears, to weep, to weep with
To outwardly express one's grief, to mourn
To bear the weight of guilt or moral responsibility
G3996.detail:
1. To grieve means to experience deep sadness. It is the feeling of one who suffers from a loss or misfortune. Jesus calls "blessed are those who mourn," meaning those who feel sorrow (Matthew 5:4) — a legitimate sadness that can lead to comfort.

2. Weeping often goes hand in hand with grieving. It is the expression of tears that accompanies pain. Mark reports that those who followed Jesus "were grieving and weeping" after his death (Mark 16:10): the two acts, internal and external, go together.

3. Mourning is to publicly express one's grief, through fasting, clothing, or gestures. Luke mentions those who will be "mourning and weeping" (Luke 6:25): a visible condition of pain and suffering.

4. To grieve can also mean to feel a pang of conscience, a sense of guilt. Paul asks the Corinthians to grieve over the serious sin committed in their assembly (1 Corinthians 5:2): it is not about tears, but about moral pain in the face of evil.
G3996.origine: The Greek verb πενθέω comes from a root that evokes the idea of pain and sorrow. In Hebrew, the word אָבַל (meaning "to weep, to mourn") expresses the same reality: the visible and internal manifestation of mourning in biblical cultures. The word is related to other Greek terms describing emotional suffering. It is a common verb in Scripture to speak of human grief in the face of death or sin.
G3996.emploi: The verb πενθέω appears about ten times in the New Testament, primarily in the Gospels and the epistles of Paul. It first describes ordinary grief: that of the disciples after Jesus' death (Mark 16:10), or the legal sorrow of those who will be deprived of food (Luke 6:25). It also expresses just sadness in the face of sin: Paul exhorts the Church to grieve over unrepentant sin within it (1 Corinthians 5:2), and he himself weeps over those who have not repented (2 Corinthians 12:21). Finally, it depicts the cosmic grief of the inhabitants of the earth at the end of times (Revelation 18:11, 15, 19). The word thus carries a spiritual significance: grief can be a path to comfort, or a sign of moral conscience.
G3996.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that sadness in the face of misfortune and sin is not forbidden — it is even blessed. Jesus declares blessed those who mourn, promising that they will be comforted (Matthew 5:4): this means that pain, when it is just, is the path to grace. This word also invites a grieving over sin, not out of sterile guilt, but out of love for justice and repentance. It is a spiritual weapon: to recognize evil and be saddened by it is already to begin to turn away from it.

sens: State of deep affliction and sorrow in the face of a loss, particularly death
Visible manifestation of mourning: dark clothing, tears, change in appearance
Moral pain, inner grief and sadness
Absence of joy and comfort
G3997.detail:
1. Mourning is the intense affliction that grips one who has lost someone or something precious. It is the deep sorrow of the heart. In James 4:9, believers are called to "feel their misery" by putting themselves "in mourning and tears": this is about sincerely recognizing the weight of one's faults and trials.

2. Mourning is visibly manifested: flowing tears, joy disappearing, expression of sadness on the face. The text says "let your laughter be turned to mourning," showing the brutal contrast between the lightness of one who laughs and the gravity of one who suffers.

3. In Revelation 18, mourning is a pain that accompanies condemnation: Babylon, which was proud, will receive in return "mourning," meaning pain and destruction. Mourning comes for those who refuse to repent.

4. In heaven, mourning will completely disappear: "There will be no more... mourning" (Revelation 21:4). God "will wipe away every tear," which means that comfort will definitively replace affliction.
G3997.origine: The Greek word penthos comes from a root meaning "to be overwhelmed" or "to be filled with pain." It translates the Hebrew evel (אֵבֶל), which refers to ritual mourning in Israel. Unlike some Greek contexts where mourning was a loud and theatrical manifestation, in Hebrew and biblical Greek, mourning is a reality of the heart that affects the whole person, both morally and physically.
G3997.emploi: The word appears four times, all in the New Testament. In James 4:9, it invites believers to move from superficial laughter to sincere mourning of repentance. In Revelation 18:7-8, mourning is the divine consequence: Babylon, which indulged in luxury, will experience mourning and plagues in return. Finally, in Revelation 21:4, mourning disappears in heaven, where God definitively comforts His own. The word always emphasizes an authentic reaction to a serious reality: sin to acknowledge, judgment to endure, or comfort to receive.
G3997.portee: Mourning calls the believer to sincerity: no false joy, no superficial laughter as long as one refuses to see their sin. It is an invitation to honest repentance. But mourning is not final: for those who believe, the promise of Revelation 21:4 assures that God will wipe away all mourning forever. Between sincere repentance here and eternal comfort in heaven, mourning connects the believer to the reality of their state and the hope of their redemption.

sens: Lacking money and essential goods
Living in material deprivation
Figuratively: spiritually or morally destitute
G3998.detail: 1. The word designates someone who has no money, who is in material need. In Luke 21:2, Jesus sees a poor widow who can only put in two small coins in the Temple treasury: she has so little that her offerings are minimal, yet she gives all that she has. 2. More broadly, it is the state of one who lives in deprivation, without resources to live with dignity. The biblical context shows that God has a particular concern for the poor. 3. By extension, the word can evoke a poverty that is not only material: that of one who knows they are spiritually destitute, lacking their own righteousness, and who relies solely on God for their salvation.
G3998.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to lack" or "to be in need." It belongs to the family of Greek words that express poverty and deprivation. The Greek uses this term to translate the Hebrew "poor," particularly in Proverbs and the book of Exodus, to designate one who has nothing and depends on the charity and kindness of others.
G3998.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 21:2. Jesus uses it to describe the widow who makes her offering at the Temple: despite her extreme poverty, she gives generously. This account makes material poverty the backdrop for an act of faith and trust in God. In the Hebrew and Greek biblical tradition, the poor are those who deserve protection and compassion, those whom God turns to with favor.
G3998.portee: This scene of the poor widow teaches that the value of an offering is not measured by its material quantity, but by the love and sacrifice of the one making it. Poverty, in the Bible, often reveals true faith: one who has nothing to offer but themselves learns to depend on God and trust in His providence. For the Christian reader, this passage invites seeking a generosity of heart rather than a wealth of goods.

sens: the number of five occurrences
five successive occurrences of the same event
G3999.detail:
1. The word simply designates the number five repeated: an action that occurs on five different occasions. In 2 Corinthians 11:24, Paul enumerates the trials he has endured for the Gospel and states that he received "five times" the punishment from the Jews (forty lashes minus one), meaning that this brutal event was repeated five times during his ministry.
2. By extension, this emphasizes the accumulation or repetition of the same painful situation — not just once, but several times in succession. The adverb highlights the intensity and persistence of what Paul has endured, transforming each isolated blow into a testimony of steadfastness in suffering.
G3999.origine: The Greek word πεντάκις combines πέντε (penta, five) and the suffix -άκις (-akis), which forms adverbs of repetition or number of times. This suffix appears in other expressions in the New Testament to count iterations ("twice," "three times"). The image is that of the number five applied not to objects, but to successive moments of the same trial.
G3999.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 11:24. Paul uses it to document a concrete detail of his personal history and commitment in ministry. Although rare, it illustrates how biblical writers use numerical adverbs to emphasize the succession and repetition of a trial, transforming a simple account of suffering into a portrait of faithfulness despite obstacles.
G3999.portee: This verse reminds the Christian that the life of a disciple is not guaranteed to be easy, but may involve repeated and serious trials. Paul exposes his struggle not to complain, but to affirm that the grace of Christ supports those who persevere — even through sufferings that return multiple times. It is a lesson of hope anchored in the concrete reality of practiced faith.
